title: fix(go-didcomm)!: validate and bind the JWE header, and take the local DID from the opening identity
body:
## Summary

`trust-tasks-go/didcomm` opened authcrypt JWEs without checking most of the header:

- `apu`/`apv` base64url errors were discarded, which turned them into empty KDF inputs.
- `apu` was never compared with `skid`, and `apv` was never recomputed from the recipient kids. The per-recipient `kid`s are unprotected, and `apv` is what binds them to the protected header.
- A single recipient entry with no `kid` was treated as addressed to us.
- `Transport.Local` was taken from that unprotected `kid`. An envelope whose `kid` had been removed in transit still opened, with `Transport.Local == ""`.
- `crit`, `zip`, `typ`, a shared `unprotected` header and extra per-recipient header parameters were ignored.
- The plaintext `from`/`to` were never compared with the envelope.

## Changes

`UnpackTrustTask` / `unpackAuthcrypt`, following DIDComm v2 and RFC 7515/7516:

- **Recipient binding.** Every recipient entry must carry a `kid`, and `apv` must equal `base64url(SHA-256(sorted recipient kids joined by "."))`, the convention the packer and affinidi use. Only the entry whose `kid` is exactly the identity's `Kid` is opened. The unlabelled-entry fallback is removed.
- **Transport.Local** is `bareDID(identity.Kid)`, the identity the caller opened the envelope with. It is never a value read from the envelope.
- **Sender binding.** `apu` must be `base64url(skid)`. Malformed base64url in `apu` or `apv` is refused.
- **Structure** (`FailNotAuthcrypt`). The following are refused:
  - `crit` or `zip` in the protected header
  - a `typ` other than `application/didcomm-encrypted+json` (an absent `typ` is accepted)
  - the RFC 7516 JSON members this profile does not process: `unprotected`, `aad`, and the flattened `header`/`encrypted_key`
  - a per-recipient header that repeats a protected parameter (RFC 7516 §7.2.1 requires them to be disjoint), or that carries `crit`/`zip`
  - JWE or protected-header member names that differ only by case (encoding/json reads them as one member, other libraries do not)

  Members RFC 7516 does not define are still ignored, as it requires.
- **Plaintext from/to.** These are inside the AEAD. A `from` whose DID is not the authenticated sender's is `FailDecrypt`. A `to` that does not name the recipient's DID is `FailNotForThisRecipient`, and an empty `"to": []` names no one and is refused the same way. Both members are still optional: an absent `to` (or `null`) is accepted.

The header checks run before the sender is resolved, so a malformed envelope never reaches `ResolveSender`.

## Behaviour changes (R3.6)

- These envelopes were opened before and are refused now: one whose recipient entry has no `kid` or a rewritten `kid`, one whose `apu`/`apv` do not name the skid / recipient kids or are not base64url, and any of the structural cases above.
- A plaintext `from` naming another DID, or a `to` not naming the recipient, is now refused.
- `Transport.Local` can no longer be empty or differ from the opening identity.
- Envelopes packed by this module, and by `affinidi-messaging-didcomm` (the existing `testdata/authcrypt-interop.fixture.json`), still open. The Rust and Dart bindings use affinidi's library, so this PR does not change them.
- No exported Go API changes. `!` is scoped to `go-didcomm` because previously accepted input is now refused.
- Consumers: I searched verifiable-trust-infrastructure, cierge, vti-didcomm-js, pnm-browser-plugin, pnm-relay, vti-message-bridge, affinidi-trust-registry-rs and openvtc. None imports `trust-tasks-go/didcomm`.

## Tests

The new file `trust-tasks-go/didcomm/jwe_header_test.go` has a test-only sealer that builds a correctly encrypted envelope from an arbitrary protected header and JSON structure. Each case therefore fails on the one thing it changes, and the test asserts the refusal's detail:

- `TestJWEHeaderMembersAreValidated`: 17 refused shapes
- `TestJWEHeaderAcceptsWhatDIDCommAllows`: no `typ`, an unknown top-level member, an unknown per-recipient parameter
- `TestJWEHeaderAPVCoversEveryRecipient`: two recipients; dropping one entry breaks `apv`
- `TestRecipientKidCannotBeStrippedOrRewritten`: stripped or relabelled `kid` is refused, and `Transport.Local` is the opening identity
- `TestPlaintextFromAndToMustMatchTheEnvelope`

`interop_multi_test.go` (review follow-up) uses `testdata/authcrypt-interop-multi.fixture.json`, a JWE packed by `affinidi-messaging-didcomm` 0.15.8 to bob and carol. Carol's entry comes first, so the entries are not in `apv`'s sorted order. The test opens the JWE as each recipient, checks that affinidi's `apv` is SHA-256 of the sorted kids, and checks that dropping an entry fails the `apv` check. This pins the check against another implementation's computation, not only against `computeAPV`. The generator source is in `testdata/README.md`. A comment referred to `scripts/gen-didcomm-interop-fixture`, which never existed, and now points at the README.

I checked the new tests against `main`'s `jwe.go`/`envelope.go`: all four new failing-case tests fail there.

In `trust-tasks-go/didcomm`, `gofmt -l .` is empty, and `go vet ./...` and `go test -race ./...` exit 0. The existing tests pass, including the affinidi interop tests.

## Parity follow-ups (not in this PR)

- An `apv` check in affinidi's decrypt, upstream. The Rust and Dart bindings decrypt through it.
- The `from`/`to` checks in the Rust (`trust-tasks-didcomm`) and Dart (`trust_tasks_didcomm`) bindings.

## Checklist (dev guide §9)

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): n/a, no clients
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1): n/a. Refusals happen before the pipeline and before `ResolveSender` is called.
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4): n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): refusals are typed `*EnvelopeError`s, not panics
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*): no new wire types. JOSE members that change an envelope's meaning are refused (R3.2), and unknown non-JOSE members are ignored, as RFC 7516 requires. The behaviour change is listed above (R3.6).
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*): no config
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*): `Transport.Local` now reports only the identity that opened the envelope
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): no mutations
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers: none

title: feat(vta/webs/dids/create): DID classes, service DIDs and DID templates (0.2)
body:
`vta/webs/dids/create/0.2`, and the family conventions at `vta/webs/_shared/0.2`. 0.1 is unchanged (now superseded).

## What changes

**1. DID classes and service DIDs.** `didClass` is REQUIRED: `relationship`, `persona` or `service` (VTI-KEY-190 – 193). A `service` did:webs — the durable identity of the VTA, a VTC, a VTN, a host service or an integration (VTI-KEY-192) — is allowed at key assurance level 1 as an **optional, alpha** method, following the amendment of VTI-KEY-001 / VTI-KEY-003 tracked in trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#120. Levels 2 – 3 stay with `vta/dids/create` and the `webs` profile.
- `serviceDidNotPermitted` now means only "this VTA's configuration does not enable did:webs service DIDs" (a separate switch from `methodDisabled`, off by default while alpha).
- New `didClassConflict` (`details.requiredClass`) holds VTI-KEY-193: a persona/relationship DID that would become a node's identity (primary of a service context), or a service DID replacing a persona primary.
- Conventions §1.1: peers that have not declared did:webs resolution may not verify a service did:webs; operators SHOULD keep a did:webvh / did:scid identity for them.

**2. DID templates.** `template`, `templateContext`, `templateVars`, as `vta/webvh/dids/create/1.2` takes them; exclusive (in the schema, via `dependentSchemas`) of `addMediatorService`, `addTspService`, `additionalServices` and `alsoKnownAs`. The VTA renders the template, then maps the rendered document onto the did:webs derivation (Conventions §9.2):
- honoured: one Ed25519 signing key in `authentication` + `assertionMethod`; one X25519 key-agreement key in `keyAgreement` (as its designation); `service` entries as designated services (ids reduced to fragments; the template may define `#didcomm` / `#tsp`); `alsoKnownAs` DIDs as designated aliases after the DID; `kind` recorded as the integration kind; `@context` ignored; `defaults` not applied.
- refused with `templateNotRepresentable` (`details.reason` ∈ `keyRoleTemplate`, `keyAlgorithm`, `documentId`, `controller`, `verificationMethod`, `verificationRelationship`, `keyAgreementRequired`, `service`, `alias`, `documentMember`; `details.members` JSON Pointers): schemaVersion 3, extra/unpublished key slots or algorithms without ed25519/x25519, further verification methods, capability relationships, no key agreement key, non-DID aliases, any other top-level member.
- `templateNotFound`, `templateVarsInvalid` (names reused from `vta/webvh/dids/create` / `provision/integration`).
- `{DID}` is the final DID: the VTA computes the inception event first (it carries no services), renders, checks, and only then commits keys.
- Response adds `didClass` (required), `template`, `templateScope`, `templateKind`.

Of the built-ins, `dtg-witness`, `did-host-*`, `ai-agent`, `push-gateway`, `trust-registry`, `ballot-box`, `room*`, `vtc-group` map whole; `vtc-host` (a third verification method), `swiyu-verifier` (P-256, unpublished update key, `profile_version`) and `vta-admin` (no key agreement) are refused.

`vta/webs/_shared/0.2/webs-records.schema.json` adds `WebsDidClass` and an optional `didClass` on `WebsDidRecord`; the slot-path and service shapes are unchanged.

## Validation
- `npm run validate`, `npm run build`
- `npm run check-bindings` (1387 specs, all four languages agree), `npm run check-published-schemas`
- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt`, `npm run build-{ts,go,dart}-bindings`
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --no-default-features --features vta,validate --test conformance webs`
- `tsc --noEmit` (trust-tasks-ts), `go vet ./specs/vta/webs/...`, `dart analyze lib/specs/vta/webs`

## Open questions
- `didClass` is a closed enum without `integration`: VTI-KEY-192 makes an integration's identity a service DID. 0.1 treated "integration" DIDs as non-service; is the reclassification right?
- `keyAgreementRequired`: a template without `keyAgreement` is refused because `WebsDidRecord` (get/list 0.1) requires a key-agreement key. Make it optional in a later get/list?
- Strict relationships: a template putting the signing key in only one of `authentication` / `assertionMethod` is refused rather than widened to both.
- Service DID adoption (setting the VTA's DID, provisioning a community) is left to those tasks; they MAY adopt only a `service`-class did:webs.
- Follow-ups: `get`/`list` 0.2 to return `didClass` and the template provenance; `update` 0.2 for template-shaped re-designation.

title: spec(rooms): purpose of use on room reads and authority credentials (VTI-ACL-102, -110)
body:
Closes the rooms gap recorded in the VTI specification's Appendix F (trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#116), following `vta/memory`'s purpose model (#1074).

**New versions**, each `extends` its predecessor:
- `rooms/keys/open/0.3` and `rooms/keys/read/0.3` add an optional `purpose`. A request whose purpose isn't granted is refused with `purposeNotGranted` (details `purposeNamed` / `purpose`, as `vta/memory/get` 0.2). The granted purposes are those both the caller's ACL entry and the principal's room authority grant. `read` passes the purpose on to the host.
- `rooms/keys/file-key/0.3` adds the same as `purposeOfUse`, because `purpose` already means seal or open. Only `open` is purpose-bound.
- `rooms/records/get/0.4` adds an optional `purpose`. The host holds a read to the purposes the presented chain states (VTI-ACL-110), and a chain that states none grants `any`.
- `rooms/owner/issue-authority/0.3` adds an optional `purposes` (`PurposeScope` from `acl/_shared/0.3`), stated in the credential. Absent means `any`.

**In place, additive:** `rooms/_shared/0.2` gains `RecordPurpose` only. The chain rule is in `rooms/owner/issue-authority/0.3`, *Purposes along a chain*: a link that states no purposes takes its parent's, and a link that states wider ones is refused whole (VTI-ACL-107). Putting it in `AuthorityPresentation`'s shared description changed a TypeScript interface every version shares, which is an API break.

**Judgement calls:**
- `browse` returns metadata only, so it isn't purpose-bound.

title: fix(mux/grant): unknown-key rule fails closed on direct authentication; no exemption for a grant without recorded keys
body:
Prose only in `messaging/mux/grant/0.1`; no schema or digest change.

A security review of the mediator implementation found that the rule as written could be switched off. The spec said an active grant stored without recorded key-agreement keys gives no basis for comparison, and that a direct DIDComm authentication does not fire the rule while one exists. One such grant, for example one stored while the resolver was down, therefore exempted every grant on the DID.

Changes:
- **A grant is never stored without its key-agreement keys.** If the member DID cannot be resolved to read them, the grant is refused with `messaging/mux:didUnresolvable`. An empty set means the document listed none, so that DID's first key-agreement key is unknown.
- **The comparison is with the keys every active grant recorded together.** A grant that recorded none no longer exempts the others.
- **Direct authentication fails closed.** The mediator MUST apply the rule, commit any suspension and detach its members before the authentication succeeds. If it cannot, it MUST refuse the authentication as retryable. A DID with no active grants is not affected.

Implementation: affinidi/affinidi-messaging-mediator branch `fix/mux-unknown-key-fail-closed`.

title: feat(acl): purpose of use on grants and on memory reads (AclEntry 0.3; vta/memory put/delete/list 0.3, get 0.2)
body:
Wire shapes for purpose of use (VTI-ACL-100 – 110, trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#115). Implementation tracking: OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#2120.

An access-control entry says who may do what, where and until when, but not
what for. An agent granted a read of its principal's memory can use the content
for anything, and nothing records the use it intended. The VTI specification
now requires the purpose (VTI-ACL-100 – 110, trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#115);
these are the wire shapes.

acl/_shared/0.3 — AclEntry 0.3 adds one REQUIRED axis, `purposes`:
`{"scope": "any"}` or `{"scope": "listed", "purposes": [...]}` with at least
one `Purpose` — a lowerCamelCase name registered in the VTI purpose registry
(personalisation, taskExecution, analytics, modelTraining) or an absolute IRI
such as a DPV purpose. `any` never grants `modelTraining`. Delegated purposes
are a subset of the granter's. CONVENTIONS.md §8a maps a 0.2 entry onto 0.3
(`any`, the authority it already held, now stated) and §12 states the rules.

acl tasks on AclEntry 0.3: grant/0.3, update/0.3, show/0.3, revoke/0.3,
change-role/0.3, list/0.4. New errors on grant and update: `purposeOutsideDelegator`
(purposes wider than the granter's) and `purposeRefused` (policy will not grant
a purpose, refused by name, never dropped). update/0.3 replaces `purposes`
wholesale; narrowing it is an audited privilege reduction. `purposes` is never
redacted by show or list. No `extends`: a REQUIRED member on the entry cannot
be added to a version a 0.2 consumer still reads.

vta/memory put/0.3, delete/0.3, list/0.3, get/0.2 (each `extends` its
predecessor) add an optional `purpose` (`MemoryPurpose`, new in
vta/_shared/0.1/memory-record, a reference to acl's `Purpose`) and a
`purposeNotGranted` error that discloses nothing and is distinct from
`contextForbidden`. A recall, and a listing with values, is purpose-bound:
refused for a purpose the entry does not grant, or for none under an entry
listing several, and audited with its purpose either way. A write is not
purpose-bound, but a conflict that returns `currentValue` is: the value is
withheld unless the request's purpose is granted.

Data rooms (a room authority credential's `purposes`, VTI-ACL-110) are a
follow-up.

Samples in other specs that named the superseded acl versions now name the new
ones, with `purposes` on every embedded entry; prose links were moved by
`npm run fix-stale-references`.


## Out of scope
- **Data rooms**: `purposes` on a room authority credential and a `purpose` on room reads (VTI-ACL-110) come in a follow-up PR.
- `acl/swap-key/0.1` still returns an AclEntry 0.1 and is unchanged.

## Checks run locally
- `npm run validate`: 1363 specs; no stale references; 23 declared extensions checked.
- `npm run check-bindings`: Rust, TS, Go and Dart agree.
- `npm run check-published-schemas`: 23 released files changed only additively.

title: fix(messaging/mux): direct authentication is compared with keys of its own relationship; grantsExpiring for every unrenewed grant
body:
Two fixes to the draft `messaging/mux` specs, found while implementing them in the Affinidi mediator. Both are prose-only: no schema, binding or digest changes.

## 1. Unknown-key rule: compare like with like (`grant/0.1`)

The rule compared "the DIDComm authcrypt sender key" with "the verification methods that signed [the member's] active grants". Authcrypt proves a `keyAgreement` key, while grants are signed with `authentication` keys. The two sets hold different keys, so taken literally **every direct login of a member DID suspends all its grants**.

The known keys are now two sets, both read from the active grants:
- **Signing keys:** the `authentication` methods that signed the grants. These are compared with grant and attach signatures, and with the TSP sender VID's signing key.
- **Key-agreement keys:** the member's `keyAgreement` methods recorded, by key material, when each grant was stored. These are compared with the DIDComm authcrypt sender key.

So a member that already logs in directly with a key it listed when it granted doesn't suspend its own grants. A key added since then (a new controller's key, or a rotation) is unknown. That matches the rule's intent: it detects a hand-over.

## 2. `grantsExpiring`: the mediator can't see a renewal opt-in (`notice/0.1`)

Producer rule 5 said to send `grantsExpiring` "only for grants whose renewal the application did not opt into". That opt-in is client-side and never reaches the mediator. The rule now says:
- send it for every grant past about 75% of its lifetime that is still active and not replaced;
- the notice MAY be stored lazily: at the principal's next authentication or connection, or on a periodic check while it's connected;
- it is never stored for a grant that is expired, revoked, suspended or replaced.

The consumer rule now says a client that renews a grant itself discards the notice for it.

Both are draft specs, so this changes them in place without a version bump.

title: feat(vtc/badges): claim codes and the badge rule counts (VTI-BDG-015, VTI-BDG-025 – 027)
body:
Phase 4 of VTC badges (VTI chapter: trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#108).

- **`vtc/badges/claims/{create,list,withdraw,redeem}/0.1`** — claim codes for events. An owner (or `vtc.badges.admin`) issues a code: at least 128 random bits the community generates, answered once, kept only as a digest, with a label, a time (at most 90 days ahead) and a claim limit. An active member redeeming it is admitted as on an approved request (VTI-BDG-024): credential first, then an accepted award whose giver is the code's issuer. Unknown, expired, exhausted, withdrawn and retired-badge codes all answer `codeInvalid`; `alreadyClaimed` and `alreadyHeld` refuse a second claim. Withdrawing stops further claims; claims made stand. The list never answers a code.
- **`_shared/0.1/badge.schema.json`**: `ClaimId`, `ClaimSecret`, `ClaimCode`.
- **`groups/_shared/0.1` `RuleCondition`**: appends the facts `kudosReceived`, `ideasSelected`, `electionTickets` and the op `atLeast` (integer `value`). `vtc/groups/create` refuses them for any group but a badge's; `vtc/badges/create` lets an automatic badge's rule read them. `electionTickets` counts tickets the community issued — never whether a ballot was cast (VTI-VOT-001).

All additive, on drafts. Bindings regenerated in their own commit; `validate`, `check-bindings` (1340 specs agree), `build`, `build-bundles` and `check-bundles` pass locally.

title: feat(auth/step-up): requests/show — the subject's wallet fetches a step-up refused to a delegated producer (auth/step-up/requests/show/0.1)
body:
## Why

A step-up refusal carries its request inline (`approve-request/0.5`, *Inline delivery*). That works only when the operation's producer can gather the evidence itself.

A producer acting with a **delegated** key cannot. Examples are an AI assistant over an MCP bridge, or an automation. It can redeem a recorded step-up but never make one. It also cannot hand the inline request to the person's wallet, because the inline request carries no proof.

## What

A new task, `auth/step-up/requests/show/0.1`.

- **The hand-off.** Beside `details.stepUpRequest`, the relying party MAY carry `details.stepUpHandoff` (`$defs.Handoff`). It holds a single-use handle of at least 128 bits, an `expiresAt`, and this task's Type URI.
- **The read.** The person's approver agent sends the handle. It receives the relying party's own **signed** `approve-request/0.5`, addressed to the subject, with the same challenge and `boundTo`. It also receives the operation, exactly as received.
- **The answer.** The agent verifies the proof and shows the operation, not only the reason. It recomputes `boundTo` where it knows the construction. It answers with `approve-response/0.7`, signed by the subject's DID, directly to the relying party.
- **The redeem.** The producer resends the identical operation, and the recorded step-up is redeemed. Nothing about redeeming changes.

A handle is answered at most once, atomically. Unknown, spent, expired and settled handles all return the single code `notFound`. Reading a handle is never part of an approval.

## Checks

- `npm run validate` and `npm run build` are clean for this spec.
- All four bindings were regenerated. `npm run check-bindings` reports that all agree.
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --all-features --test conformance` passed 3785 tests.

## Follow-up

The VTI specification will name the trigger-link flow that carries the handle to the wallet (`/vti/flow/step-up/0.1`, in the links chapter). VTI will then implement it in the VTC, the browser plugin and `vtc-mcp`.

title: fix(cli)!: refuse a plain-http registry unless it is on loopback or --allow-http-registry is given
body:
## Summary

`trust-tasks` accepted a plain `http://` registry (from `--registry`, `TRUST_TASKS_REGISTRY` or the manifest's `registry`), while `[sources.<name>]` were already https-only. The registry's `specs/index.json` supplies the digests that `add`/`update` pin, so over http the network path could supply both the digest and the bundle it names.

- `Registry::open` now refuses an `http://` registry unless its host is loopback (`localhost`, `127.0.0.0/8`, `[::1]`) or the new global `--allow-http-registry` flag is given (which prints a warning).
- The agent for an `https://` registry or source is built with `https_only(true)`, so an https origin cannot redirect a fetch to http.
- README and `--registry` help updated.

## Behaviour change (R3.6)

A non-loopback `http://` registry that used to be fetched is now refused with an error naming `--allow-http-registry`. `https://`, `file://`, directory and loopback-http registries behave as before. Hence `fix(cli)!`.

## Tests

- `registry.rs` unit tests: host extraction, loopback detection, refusal/acceptance matrix.
- `tests/cli.rs`: `a_plain_http_registry_is_refused_unless_loopback_or_allowed`.

Not run locally; relying on CI.

## Checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2) — agent keeps its 120 s global timeout
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3) — n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1) — refusal happens before any fetch or write
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4) — n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5) — n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6) — n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*) — no wire types
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*) — http needs an explicit flag
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*)
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1) — no mutation added
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers — none

title: chore(deps): pin prettier at the root to the version trust-tasks-ts-gen uses
body:
Adds `prettier` 3.8.3 to the root `devDependencies`, the same exact version `trust-tasks-ts-gen` pins. The root lockfile already resolved 3.8.3 transitively, so nothing changes today.

Why: the generated TypeScript bindings are formatted with prettier. While the root only had it transitively, a Dependabot bump in `trust-tasks-ts-gen` left the root on the old version and `build-ts-bindings drift` / `trust-tasks-gen-ts equivalence` failed (seen on #1184). With a direct pin, the `ts-generator` group added in #1188 moves both together; such a PR still needs `npm run build-ts-bindings` committed if the new prettier reformats output.

No package API or behaviour change.

title: fix(https,dart-https)!: cap HTTPS client responses, keep bearer tokens on https, stop following redirects, and keep response bodies out of errors
body:
## Summary

Resource limits and transport rules for the two HTTPS clients: Rust `trust-tasks-https::HttpsClient` and Dart `trust_tasks_https`'s `HttpsClient`.

| | Rust | Dart |
|---|---|---|
| Response size cap | `max_response_bytes` (default `DEFAULT_MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES` = 256 KiB). Read chunk by chunk and refused past the cap; a declared `Content-Length` over the cap is refused before reading. New `ClientError::ResponseTooLarge { limit }`. | `maxResponseBytes` (default `defaultMaxResponseBytes` = 256 KiB), same behaviour. New `ResponseTooLargeException`. |
| Scheme | `server_url` must be https. Plain http is accepted for a loopback host (`localhost`, `127.0.0.0/8`, `[::1]`), or with `allow_insecure_http(true)`. A bearer token is never sent over non-loopback http, so `build()` returns `Config`. | Same rules: `allowInsecureHttp`, and the constructor throws `ArgumentError`. |
| Redirects | `Policy::none()` by default, so a 3xx is `HttpStatus`. `follow_redirects(true)` follows same-origin redirects only, at most 5. An https client is built `https_only`. | `followRedirects = false`. A platform client that followed anyway (a browser's fetch) is detected through `BaseResponseWithUrl.url` and refused. |
| Error text | `HttpStatus` no longer prints the body; its `body` field keeps at most 512 bytes. `ResponseDecode` keeps only serde's category and line/column, because serde messages can quote values. | `HttpStatusException.body` is truncated to 512 chars (it was never in `toString`). `ResponseDecodeException.toString` names only the cause's type, because `FormatException` quotes the source. |
| Exceptions | n/a | Every error from the HTTP client is wrapped as `TransportException`. Previously only `TimeoutException` and `ClientException` were wrapped, so e.g. a TLS `HandshakeException` escaped the sealed hierarchy. |
| Timeout | (reqwest's timeout already covers the body) | `timeout` now covers reading the body as well, and cancels the read when it fires. |
| Response verifier | n/a | `responseVerifier` without `serverVid` throws `ArgumentError`, because a proof only says who signed. |

## Behaviour changes (R3.6)

- A non-loopback `http://` server URL is refused unless explicitly allowed. With a bearer token it is always refused.
- Redirects are no longer followed by default (Rust). The Dart VM client also stops following them, and the web client's followed redirects are refused.
- Responses over 256 KiB fail.
- `HttpStatus` / `ResponseDecode` text changes, and stored bodies are truncated.
- Dart: new sealed subclass `ResponseTooLargeException`, so exhaustive switches need an arm (the example is updated). Some exceptions that used to escape raw are now `TransportException`. `responseVerifier` requires `serverVid`.
- Rust: a new `ClientError` variant.

Hence `!` scoped to `https` and `dart-https`.

## Overlap

#1204 (this crate's response-proof change) also edits `trust-tasks-https/src/client.rs`, and `git merge-tree` reports a textual conflict there. Whichever merges second needs a rebase; the changes are independent. #1204 also makes `ClientError` `#[non_exhaustive]`.

## Tests

- Rust (`tests/end_to_end.rs`):
  - `a_plain_http_server_url_is_refused_unless_loopback_or_allowed`
  - `redirects_are_not_followed_by_default` (asserts the redirect target is never hit)
  - `a_response_over_max_response_bytes_is_refused`
  - `client_errors_do_not_quote_the_response_body`
- Dart (`test/client_test.dart`, group `transport limits`): scheme and loopback rules, token over http, verifier without server VID, redirects not followed, streamed and declared over-cap bodies, arbitrary client errors becoming `TransportException`, error text not quoting the body.

Not run locally; relying on CI. `dart format --language-version=3.3` was applied, matching CI.

## Checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): the Dart timeout now covers the body read
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1): n/a
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4): redirects (a re-POST) are off by default
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*): no wire change
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*): https-only, no redirects and the size cap are defaults
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*)
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): no mutations
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers: none

title: fix(go-proof)!: decode documents as I-JSON and refuse out-of-range ECDSA private keys
body:
## Summary

Two input checks in the Go proof module (`trust-tasks-go/proof`).

### The verifier and signer decode documents as I-JSON

`decode` used `encoding/json`, which accepts input that RFC 8785 (via I-JSON, RFC 7493) says to refuse, and rewrites it on the way in:

- invalid UTF-8 and an unpaired surrogate escape (`"\ud800"`) both become U+FFFD;
- of two members with the same name, the last one is kept;
- `Decoder.Decode` stops after the first value and ignores what follows.

Each one lets a different byte string canonicalize to the same JCS input. A document signed over `"admin�"` still verified after the value was changed to `"admin\ud800"`. A document with `"role":"owner","role":"admin"` verified under a proof over `"role":"admin"`, though a reader that keeps the first member sees `owner`.

`decode` now refuses all four, before any key is resolved:

- `utf8.Valid` over the whole input;
- a scan of string literals that requires each `\uD800`–`\uDBFF` escape to be followed directly by a `\uDC00`–`\uDFFF` escape, and refuses a low-surrogate escape on its own;
- a `json.Decoder` token walk that refuses two members of one object whose names are equal after unescaping (`"a"` and `"a"` count as the same), at any depth;
- anything after the first value other than whitespace.

The verifier reports these as `malformedProof`, and `Sign` returns an error.

### `SignerFromPrivateKey` checks ECDSA private keys

The constructor passed any byte string to `elliptic.Curve.ScalarBaseMult`. An empty, all-zero or 5-byte P-256 key gave a `Signer` with a plausible `did:key`. A zero key failed only at `Sign`, and a 5-byte key signed.

It now requires exactly 32 (P-256) or 48 (P-384) bytes, and builds the key with `crypto/ecdh`'s `NewPrivateKey`, which refuses a scalar of 0 or ≥ n. The public key comes from `ecdh`, not the deprecated `ScalarBaseMult`. A test checks that the derived `did:key` is unchanged. Ed25519 seeds were already length-checked.

### Other runtimes

The Rust, TypeScript and Dart verifiers take an already-parsed value (`serde_json::Value`, a JS object, a Dart `Map`), so duplicate members are resolved by the caller's JSON parser (last one wins in all three) before the verifier sees the document. A verifier there cannot see a duplicate. `serde_json` refuses an unpaired surrogate escape. TypeScript's JCS writes one as an escape (`JSON.stringify`), so it hashes differently from U+FFFD. This PR changes only Go. I did not add a shared vector because each runtime's vector runner parses the file with its own JSON parser first, so the vector would test those parsers rather than the verifiers. The Rust runner would panic on the lone-surrogate file instead of reporting `invalid`.

## Behaviour changes (R3.6)

- `proof.Verifier` refuses, as `malformedProof`, a document that is not valid UTF-8, carries an unpaired surrogate escape, repeats a member name within one object, or has trailing data. It accepted all of these before.
- `Signer.Sign` returns an error for the same inputs.
- `proof.SignerFromPrivateKey` returns an error for a P-256/P-384 key that is not exactly 32/48 bytes, or whose scalar is 0 or ≥ n. Before, it returned a signer. A caller that passed a scalar without leading zero bytes must left-pad it to the curve's length.
- No exported signature changes. The `!` is scoped to `go-proof` because previously accepted input is now refused.

## Tests

Not run locally. Remote CI runs `go vet` and `go test -race` on the module.

- `jcs_test.go`: `TestDecodeRefusesInputJCSCannotRepresentFaithfully` covers duplicates (plain, after unescaping, nested), each lone-surrogate shape, invalid and truncated UTF-8, a UTF-8-encoded surrogate, and trailing values or garbage. `TestDecodeAcceptsWellFormedInput` covers the same name in different objects, escaped surrogate pairs in either case, an escaped backslash before `u`, literal U+FFFD and astral characters, and trailing whitespace.
- `proof_test.go`: `TestVerifierRefusesInputThatDecodesLossily` signs a document, then applies the lone-surrogate, invalid-UTF-8 and duplicate-member changes to its bytes. `TestSignRefusesDuplicateMembers`. `TestSignerFromPrivateKeyRefusesInvalidEcdsaScalars` covers empty, short, ±1 byte, zero, n, n+1 and all-`0xff` keys refused, and 1, n−1 and a leading-zero key accepted, signing and verifying, for both curves. `TestSignerFromPrivateKeyPublicKeyMatchesScalarBaseMult`.

## Overlap with open PRs

`git merge-tree` against #1204, #1066 and #1206 merges cleanly. None of them touches `trust-tasks-go/proof`.

## Checklist (dev guide §9)

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): n/a, no clients
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1): n/a, no state
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4): n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*): no wire type changes. The behaviour changes are listed above (R3.6).
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*): no config. Every new check fails closed.
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*): the error names the refused construct.
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): no mutations
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers: none

title: fix(dart-https)!: screen proof DID methods to did:key by default and hold error responses to the response verifier
body:
## Summary

Brings the Dart HTTPS binding (`trust_tasks_https`) in line with the Rust crate's server DID-method default and client error-response handling (#1204).

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Server DID-method screen | `allowedDidMethods` null by default: with a `proofVerifier`, a `proof.verificationMethod` of any DID method reached the verifier | With a `proofVerifier` and no choice, only `did:key` passes (`defaultAllowedDidMethods`). `allowedDidMethods: {...}` widens it; `allowAnyDidMethod: true` lifts it (for a verifier whose resolver bounds its own egress). Passing both is an `ArgumentError`. A server with no verifier screens nothing, as before. |
| Client error responses | With a `responseVerifier`, success responses were verified but a `trust-task-error` was returned as `TrustTaskErrorException` unconditionally | A `trust-task-error` is `TrustTaskErrorException` only when its proof verifies over the body as received and its `issuer` / `recipient` are `serverVid` / `myVid`. Otherwise it is the new `UnverifiedErrorResponseException(httpStatus, reason, error)`, documented as untrusted: the document is kept for diagnostics and must not be read as the server's answer. Without a `responseVerifier`, nothing changes. |

`HttpsServer.allowedDidMethods` still reports the screen actually applied (null when nothing is screened). The example's exhaustive `switch` gains an arm for the new subclass, and the README's exception table and pipeline step are updated.

## Behaviour changes (R3.6)

- A Dart `HttpsServer` with a `proofVerifier` and no DID-method configuration now refuses proofs whose `verificationMethod` is not `did:key`, with `proofInvalid`, before the verifier runs. Deployments verifying `did:web` / `did:webvh` proofs must pass `allowedDidMethods` or `allowAnyDidMethod: true`.
- A Dart `HttpsClient` with a `responseVerifier` now throws `UnverifiedErrorResponseException` for an error document without a valid proof from the configured server.
- New subclass of the sealed `HttpsClientException`, so exhaustive `switch`es need an arm.

Hence `!` scoped to `dart-https`.

## Overlap

#1204 is Rust-only; `git merge-tree` against it reports no conflict.

## Tests

- `test/server_test.dart`, group `DID-method screen default`: the constant is `{'key'}`; with a verifier and no choice `did:web` is refused before the verifier and `did:key` passes; `allowAnyDidMethod` lifts it; an explicit set replaces it; no verifier screens nothing; both options together is an `ArgumentError`. The shared fixture opts its fake verifiers into any method, as the Rust tests do.
- `test/client_test.dart`, group `error responses with a response verifier`: unsigned, bad-proof, verifier-throws, other-issuer and other-recipient errors are `UnverifiedErrorResponseException` (status, reason and document kept; `toString` omits the code); a signed error from the server is `TrustTaskErrorException`; the verifier sees the body exactly as received; without a verifier an unsigned error is still returned.

Not run locally; relying on CI. `dart format --language-version=3.3` was applied, matching CI.

## Checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): no new clients
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1): n/a
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4): n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*): no wire change
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*): `did:key`-only is the default with a verifier; an unattested error is not treated as the server's answer
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*): `UnverifiedErrorResponseException.toString` names neither the unattested code nor message
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): no mutations
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers: none

title: fix(rs,ts,go,dart,proof,ts-proof,go-proof,dart-proof)!: refuse out-of-range timestamp fields instead of rolling them over
body:
## Summary

The four runtimes read the same `issuedAt` / `expiresAt` bytes as different instants, or as an instant in one runtime and an error in another. The proof verifiers did the same with `created`. Each runtime now matches the shared RFC 3339 pattern and then range-checks every field itself, as the proof verifiers already do for `expires`.

### Document timestamps (`issuedAt`, `expiresAt`)

The rule is the same in all four: month 1-12, a day the month has (leap years included), hour 0-23, minute and second 0-59 (no leap second), and offset hours 0-23 with minutes 0-59 (RFC 3339's `time-numoffset`).

| Runtime | Accepted before | Change |
|---|---|---|
| TypeScript `parseRfc3339` | `Date.parse` read `2026-02-30` as 2 March, `2026-04-31` as 1 May, and `T24:00:00Z` as the next day | range check before `Date.parse` |
| Dart `parseRfc3339` | `DateTime.tryParse` read `2026-13-45T25:61:61Z` as 2027-02-15, and took `+99:99` | range check before `DateTime.tryParse` |
| Go `parseTimestamp` | `time.Parse` accepted `+24:00` and `+23:60` | offset range check after `time.Parse` (it refuses the rest) |
| Rust `TrustTask` | chrono read `:60` as a leap second and accepted a space for the `T` | `issuedAt` / `expiresAt` deserialize through a strict reader (`deserialize_with`), which then hands chrono a value known to be in range |

All of these now fail as `malformedRequest`, as any unparseable timestamp already did.

### Proof `created` (all four proof verifiers)

`created` now goes through each verifier's existing `expires` parser (the `dateTimeStamp` ranges, offset at most 14:00). Before:

- **TypeScript** accepted a regex-valid but unparseable `created` (month 13): `Date.parse` gave `NaN`, `NaN > horizon` is false, and the proof passed that check. It also rolled February 30 over.
- **Dart** rolled month 13 and February 30 over.
- **Go** accepted `+24:00`.
- **Rust** left `created` to the upstream proof type (chrono), which accepts a leap second.

All four now refuse these as `malformedProof`. The now-unused `created` regexes in TS, Go and Dart are removed.

### Shared vectors

- `fixtures/consume/timestamps.json` lists 10 valid values with their `epochMs` (leap days, a fraction, ±23:59 offsets, a minute offset) and 18 invalid ones (each out-of-range field, a leap second, offsets 24:00 / 23:60 / 99:99, no zone, a space separator, a bare date). It is run by `trust-tasks-rs/tests/timestamps.rs` (through `TrustTask` deserialization, for both members), `trust-tasks-ts/test/timestamps.test.ts`, `trust-tasks-go/trusttasks/timestamps_internal_test.go` and `trust-tasks-dart/test/timestamps_test.dart`. The README describes it.
- `fixtures/proof` has five new correctly signed entries, all `invalid` for every runtime: `created-february-30`, `-hour-24`, `-month-13`, `-leap-second` and `-offset-24-hours`. They are signed with the seed-7 key. The signing code reproduced the baseline vector's `proofValue` byte for byte before generating them.

Issue #1120 proposes a shared freshness vector file (`now` / policy / `issuedAt` / `expiresAt` → verdict and record expiry). This PR covers only its calendar-invalid part. The `expiresAt`-replaces-`maxAge` disagreement it describes is a separate change.

## Behaviour changes (R3.6)

- TS, Dart, Rust and Go consumers refuse, as `malformedRequest`, an `issuedAt` / `expiresAt` they used to read as some other instant. TS: Feb 30, Apr 31, hour 24. Dart: any out-of-range field or offset. Rust: a leap second or a space separator. Go: offset hour 24 or minute 60.
- Rust: deserializing a `TrustTask` with such a timestamp now fails. JSON `null` and an absent member are still `None`.
- The TS, Dart, Go and Rust proof verifiers refuse a `created` with an out-of-range field or an offset beyond 14:00 as `malformedProof`.
- No exported signature changes. The `!` is for previously accepted input that is now refused, scoped to each package whose acceptance changed.
- Not changed: lower-case `t`/`z`. TS, Dart and Rust accept them and Go's `time.Parse` does not. That disagreement already existed and is not in the vectors. Payload-level `format: date-time` members are also not changed, because generated types read them.

## Tests

Not run locally. Remote CI runs them. The shared vectors are the main coverage. The TS file also checks two pipeline cases: an `expiresAt` of February 30 is `malformedRequest` from `validateBasic`, and an `issuedAt` of `2026-01-31T24:00:00Z` (otherwise exactly "now") is `malformedRequest` from `validateFreshness`. Rust also checks that `null` and absent timestamps still deserialize to `None`.

## Overlap with open PRs

`git merge-tree` against #1204 (which also edits `trust-tasks-proof/src/affinidi/mod.rs`), #1066, #1206, #1208 and #1209 merges cleanly.

## Checklist (dev guide §9)

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): n/a, no clients
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1): n/a. The refusal comes before any item-11 record.
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4): n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*): no wire type changes. What each runtime accepts is narrowed to the same set. The behaviour change is listed above (R3.6).
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*): no config. An out-of-range field is refused.
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*): the messages name the member that failed.
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): no mutations
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers: none

title: fix(release): raise the Dart siblings' trust_tasks floor when the Release PR takes the core across a minor
body:
Release PR #1085 fails `bindings match specs`: `check-sibling-core-ranges` reports that the five Dart siblings' `trust_tasks: ^0.9.3` does not admit the core it bumps to, `0.10.0`. This is the first Release PR to take the Dart core across a `0.x` minor since the check landed, and no release script moves those floors. #964 solved the TypeScript half by warning, but that does not fit Dart: npm siblings install the core from the registry, while Dart siblings build against the in-tree core (`pubspec_overrides.yaml`), so Dart can take the new floor in the Release PR itself.

## Change

- `scripts/raise-dart-core-floor.mjs` — rewrites a pubspec's `dependencies: trust_tasks: ^X` to `^<core>` when the range does not admit the core. It touches only that constraint, which `release-pr.sh open` already accepts, never lowers a floor, and prints the old range when it changes one.
- `release-bump-dart.sh` — for a sibling, when `TRUST_TASKS_CORE` is set, raises the floor and treats that as a reason to release, at least a patch, even with no other change. A sibling whose new floor is never published can't be used with the new core. The changelog gets a `### Dependencies` line, because no commit describes the change.
- `release-pr.sh` — passes the in-tree core version to each Dart bump (`trust_tasks` is bumped first), then raises the floor of the tested-but-unreleased `trust-tasks-dart-tsp` too.
- Tests in `scripts/test-release/release-bump-dart-floor.test.mjs`; CLAUDE.md and RELEASING.md now describe the automatic step.

## Verified

- `npm run test:release-scripts`: 33/33 pass.
- I ran the Dart half of `prepare` on a copy of `main`. It gave `trust_tasks` 0.9.37 → 0.10.0, proof/https 0.2.0 (their own breaking commits), didcomm 0.1.4, and capability_client 0.1.1 → 0.1.2 (released only for the floor). All five floors moved to `^0.10.0`, and `check-sibling-core-ranges` then passes.

On the merge of the next Release PR, the sibling `verify-dart` legs will fail until `trust_tasks` 0.10.0 is on pub.dev, as already documented. Re-run them once it is.

title: site: fix prose links, add lifecycle banners, URL-backed registry filters, 404s, error boundary, a11y and stale copy
body:
Fixes the registry-website findings from the 2026-11-11 review. Per issue below: `Closes` means fully addressed, `Part of` lists what is left.

## Status per issue

Closes #1146: relative links in spec and binding prose
- New `website/assets/routes.js` → `resolveProseHref`. It resolves each href against the prose file's served path, then maps it: `/spec/<slug>/<M.N>#frag`, `/binding/…`, `/schema/<slug>` for shared schemas, `/specification#…` for SPEC.md, the `/specs/…` asset for other published files, and GitHub for files outside the published trees. Images are made absolute too.
- A delegated click handler on `.tt-prose` sends internal links through the SPA router.
- The build now runs the same function over every link in every spec and binding (`checkProseLinksAsRendered`), so links are checked from where they render. Today that is 5165 spec, 5712 framework, 1214 schema, 1866 asset, 84 binding and 14 GitHub links, and all of them resolve.

Closes #1155: lifecycle banner and Proof requirement row
- `build-registry.mjs` computes `lifecycle: {state, successor}` per version. It uses the generators' rule: superseded means a later live version exists at equal or higher maturity. Retired and withdrawn are covered too. Today: 850 current, 468 superseded, 73 retired.
- The spec page shows a banner that links to the successor.
- The Proof requirement row uses `proofLevels()`.
- Also fixed: the classification panel's §7.3 `SpecRef` was handed a no-op `setRoute`, so clicking it did nothing.

Closes #1153: error boundary and boot fallback
- `TTErrorBoundary` is keyed on the route (registry filter changes don't remount it). The nav and footer stay alive, and the page links to GitHub.
- `#root` holds static fallback text that stays visible if the scripts fail to load or compile.

Closes #1149: navigation at narrow widths
- Below 1240px a `<button aria-expanded aria-controls>` disclosure shows the links. It closes on navigation and on Escape.
- The footer carries the full grouped link set (Specification / Build / Registry / About).
- Checked in headless Chrome at 375, 1000 and 1400px.

Closes #1150: not-found view, robots.txt and sitemap
- `NotFoundPage` is the default route, and `parsePath` is strict: an unknown name, or extra segments on a single page, is not found.
- `robots.txt` and `sitemap.xml` (1592 URLs) are generated by the build and added to `ROOT_FILES`, with `test:infra` cases.

Part of #1151: per-route title and description
- Done: `document.title` and the meta description follow the route.
- Left (parked): static per-spec HTML stubs with OG tags and canonical links.

Part of #1152: Type URI responses
- Done: the CloudFront function returns a generated JSON **404** for a JSON-only `Accept` under `/spec/` or `/ceremony/` that neither negotiation branch maps (bad slug, missing version, three-part task version, definition asked for as a schema). Browsers still get the SPA. `test:infra` and `verify.sh` cover it.
- Done: `deploy.yml` uploads `*.schema.json` as `application/schema+json`.
- Left: **CORS and `Vary: Accept`.** The distribution is not managed as code in this repo, so this needs a response-headers policy applied by hand. `infra/cloudfront/README.md` now documents the exact `create-response-headers-policy` config.
- ⚠️ The changed function also needs a manual `update-function` and `publish-function` (README → "Updating the function"). Until then the live site keeps the old routing.

Part of #1154: registry filters
- Done: filters live in the URL (`/registry/<cat>?q=&kw=&status=`, via `replaceState`). The page reads only the route, so Back/Forward and the nav "Registry" link reset it correctly.
- Done: status chips come from the statuses present (draft and retired today).
- Done: search text is precomputed, the URL update is debounced, and results show 60 at a time with a "Show more" button.
- Left (parked): virtualisation, and grouping governance by slug family.

Part of #1156: accessibility
- Done: focus moves to the page `h1` on navigation.
- Done: a skip link.
- Done: `--tt-*-text` tokens of at least 4.5:1 on cream, white and surface-alt, used for status pills, category, library and binding text. The primary button now uses violet-text (white on it is 5.7:1).
- Done: the filter headings are `h2` (they were `h5`), the search icon is `aria-hidden`, and "Copied" appears only when the clipboard write succeeds, with an `aria-live` announcement.
- Left (parked): a dark theme. It has not been checked with a screen reader.

Part of #1145: tasks.generated.js size
- Done: `tasks.generated.js` and `registry.json` are written minified (13.2 MB → 10.0 MB and 11.4 MB → 8.2 MB).
- Done: `tasks.generated.js` is uploaded **gzip-encoded** (`--content-encoding gzip`). Only the page loads it, from a `<script>` tag, so this is safe.
- Done: the page's data scripts are now `defer`, so the fallback text paints while the file downloads. Babel still runs after all deferred scripts.
- Deliberately not done: `registry.json` is **not** stored pre-encoded, because machine consumers fetch it and not every client decodes an encoding it didn't ask for. Minified it is under CloudFront's 10 MB on-the-fly compression ceiling, and the build warns at 90% of that.
- Left (parked): the structural slim index.

Part of #1148: caching
- Done: no build timestamp, so an unchanged registry gives identical bytes. `registry.json`'s `generatedAt` is replaced by `updated`, the latest spec change date. No in-repo consumer reads `registry.json`.
- Done: `Cache-Control: no-cache` on `index.html` and the assets.
- Done: `public, max-age=300, stale-while-revalidate=86400` on `/specs/**`.
- Left: content-hashed `immutable` assets, which need the bundler (#1147, parked).

Part of #1157: tests and dev server
- Done: `npm run test:website` now compiles every JSX file and `index.html`'s inline script with the integrity-checked `@babel/standalone` that `index.html` pins. After a build it also renders the app with React's server renderer across 26 routes against the real registry. It already caught a syntax error during this work.

title: ci: require a validated example per spec (ratcheted) and check runtime default parity
body:
Part of #1131. Part of #1130.

## #1131: every spec needs a validated example (ratcheted)

New lint: `scripts/lib/spec-examples.mjs`, called from `scripts/build-registry.mjs`. It covers the latest version of every slug unless that version is retired or withdrawn. That is 848 versions today.

- **Request example required.** The spec needs a fenced JSON block, anywhere in `spec.md`, whose `type` is its own Type URI (bare or `#request`).
- **Response example required.** If the schema has `$defs.Response`, the spec also needs a `#response` example.
- **Payloads validated against the spec's own schema.** Each example's `payload` is checked against the payload schema, or against `$defs.Response` for a response. Cross-file `$ref`s are resolved on disk. `checkExampleDocuments` still checks the envelope, as before.
- **Baseline.** The baseline is `scripts/lib/spec-examples-allowlist.json`. Entries are keyed by `<slug>/<version>`, so a new version of an allowlisted spec still owes its examples. It holds 179 versions and 323 findings:

  | Finding | Count |
  |---|---|
  | `missing-request` | 149 |
  | `missing-response` | 167 |
  | `invalid-request` | 4 |
  | `invalid-response` | 3 |

  The build fails on a finding that is not listed. It also fails on a listed entry that no longer applies, so the baseline can only shrink.
- **Tests.** Unit tests are in `scripts/test/spec-examples.test.mjs` and run under `npm run test:website`.

The current tree has 149 versions with no request example, not 136. The issue's 136 counted versions with no `json` block at all. The other 13 have JSON blocks, but none of those blocks is a document of the spec itself.

### Existing examples that fail their own schema (baselined with a reason, not fixed)

None of these is an obvious typo, and they are all in other owners' namespaces:

| Spec | Rule | Problem |
|---|---|---|
| `auth/passkey/login/finish/0.2` | invalid-request | Example 2 abbreviates `credential` and leaves out `id`, `rawId` and `type`. |
| `provision/integration/0.3` | invalid-request | The placeholder `holder` and `nonce` do not match the schema patterns. |
| `provision/integration/0.3` | invalid-response | The placeholder `digestMultibase` and `summary.bundleIdHex` do not match the schema patterns. |
| `rooms/blobs/get/0.2` | invalid-response | `target.url` shortens the signature to a literal `…`, which is not a valid URI. |
| `rooms/blobs/upload/begin/0.2` | invalid-response | `targets[0].url` has the same literal `…`. |
| `vault/sign-trust-task/0.2` | invalid-request | Example 2 is missing the required `entryId` and `unsignedEnvelope`, and has members the schema does not declare. |
| `vault/upsert/0.4` | invalid-request | `sealedSecret` uses an older envelope shape. |

### Parked: `extract_examples` collecting by `type`

I made the change and regenerated. The diff went well beyond conformance tests for the eight specs without headings:

- **Scope.** It touched 78 test files across about 80 specs, and added `trust_task_control` and `trust_task_ok`.
- **Renumbering.** Existing tests were renumbered in `auth/step-up/approve-response/0.4` and `0.5`.
- **Failures.** 90 of the new tests failed. 60 of those are `missing field type`, because the examples use `"proof": { "…": "…" }` placeholders. The rest are 16 round-trip mismatches, 5 pattern failures, 4 `SealedEnvelope` mismatches, and unknown fields.

Landing the change would mean editing dozens of specs in other namespaces, or adding a skip-list to the codegen. So I reverted it. The CLAUDE.md row for the new lint notes that the Rust conformance harvest still reads only the `## Request` / `## Response` sections. This is why the PR does not close #1131.

## #1130: runtime parity matrix (docs and a check; no behaviour change)

- **`docs/runtime-parity.md`.** A feature × language matrix: yes / deliberately no / todo. Each cell cites its source location. It includes the three deliberate differences CLAUDE.md already listed. CLAUDE.md now points to it in one line.
- **`check-bindings`.** It now compares the default clock skew (60 s), consequential max age (5 min), expiry horizon (30 d) and replay-guard capacity across the four runtimes. It reads them independently and does not import from the generators.
- **The issue's table is out of date.** The current tree already has the expiry horizon in all four runtimes, and the replay capacity default is **100,000** in all four, not 10,000.

These still need a decision, and are marked that way in the matrix:

- prune depth (Rust 128, TS 64, Go 256, Dart 128)
- the `extends` chain bound
- what a capacity of 0 does (Rust panics, TS throws `RangeError`, Go and Dart silently use 100,000)
- the read-as names
- whether TS and Dart should bundle a validator
- the discovery responder and `maxDocumentBytes` outside Rust

## Verification

All passed:

- `npm run validate`
- `npm run build`
- `npm run check-bindings`, which reports the four defaults agreeing. I also changed one default by hand to confirm the check fails.
- `npm run test:website`

No library code or generated output changed.

title: fix(dart-https): advertise the expiry horizon, and pin all four runtimes' freshness to shared vectors
body:
Closes #1120

## Where the issue stands

The rule change the issue asks for is already on `main`. #1163 (merged 2026-11-11, after the review that filed this issue at `1aeaaaa26`) ported Rust's rule to TypeScript, Go and Dart: a stated `expiresAt` replaces the maximum age, up to an expiry horizon (`expiryHorizonMs` / `ExpiryHorizon` / `expiryHorizon`, 30 days in the consequential policy), with the clamp on the retained record. #1163 carried the `!` for that behaviour change (`fix(rs,ts,go,dart)!`). It said the shared vector file was left for a later PR. This PR adds that file, and fixes the one place I found that still described the old behaviour.

I checked every consume path that applies freshness or computes a record expiry. They all use the policy's horizon:
- TS `consumeInbound`, Go `ConsumeInbound`, Dart `consumeInbound`: `validateFreshness` and `recordExpiry` on `checks.freshness`.
- TSP and DIDComm consumers (`trust-tasks-ts-tsp`, `trust-tasks-go/{tsp,didcomm}`, `trust-tasks-dart-{tsp,didcomm}`): they default to the consequential policy and pass it to the core pipeline.
- Dart HTTPS server: it runs `validateFreshness` early, then `consumeInbound`.

None of them has its own copy of the rule.

## What changes

**`fixtures/consume/freshness.json`: shared vectors, run by all four runtimes.** Each case gives `now`, a named policy, `issuedAt` and `expiresAt`. A runtime runs item 4's expiry check (`validateBasic`, with no recipient) and then the freshness bound. It must reach the case's `verdict` (`accept`, `expired` or `malformedRequest`). For an accepted case, the record expiry must equal `recordExpiry` (`null` means unbounded). 36 cases:
- the issue's own case: `issuedAt` 10 min ago and `expiresAt` 1 h ahead is accepted, with the record kept until `expiresAt`. The same age with no `expiresAt` is `expired`.
- the edges of every window, to the millisecond: `issuedAt + maxAge + skew`, `expiresAt` (inclusive, no skew), and `issuedAt + horizon + skew` for an `expiresAt` beyond the horizon. Each is accepted 1 ms before the edge and refused at it.
- an `expiresAt` exactly at the horizon is honoured and not clamped. One 1 ms beyond it is clamped to `horizon + skew`. One a year out is accepted inside the horizon with the record clamped.
- with no horizon, any `expiresAt` is honoured. A zero horizon clamps at `issuedAt`.
- skew: `issuedAt` exactly at `now + skew` is accepted, 1 ms more is `malformedRequest`. A zero-skew policy is covered too.
- `expiresAt` at or before `issuedAt`.
- a missing `issuedAt`, with and without `requireIssuedAt`. A document with neither timestamp is unboundable under a window and unbounded under the default policy. A missing `issuedAt` with an `expiresAt` beyond the horizon: the horizon needs an `issuedAt`, so the `expiresAt` stands.
- an `issuedAt` with an offset and one with a fraction.
- a calendar-invalid `issuedAt` and `expiresAt`. These complement `fixtures/consume/timestamps.json` from #1210.

The `default` and `consequential` policies in the file must equal each runtime's own constants. That pins the 30-day horizon, 5-minute max age and 60 s skew across all four.

Runners: `trust-tasks-rs/tests/freshness_vectors.rs`, `trust-tasks-ts/test/freshness-vectors.test.ts`, `trust-tasks-go/trusttasks/freshness_vectors_test.go`, `trust-tasks-dart/test/freshness_vectors_test.dart`. All four passed every case without any runtime change, so the runtimes agree today. `rust.yml`'s path filter gains `fixtures/**`: the Rust integration tests read it, and before this a fixture-only change ran no Rust CI.

**`trust_tasks_https` (Dart): the discovery 0.4 window states the horizon.** The server enforces `freshness.expiryHorizon` since #1163, but its `trust-task-discovery/0.4` window still left out `expiryHorizonSeconds`. That told producers the maximum age applies to every document. It now states the horizon rounded down to whole seconds, as Rust's `AcceptanceWindow::of_policy` does. A horizon under one second cannot be stated: zero is invalid in the schema, and leaving the member out would claim the wider max-age window. So no window is stated for it (responder rule 1: never advertise wider than you enforce). The 0.3 window is unchanged; it cannot carry the member and is narrower, which is permitted.

## Why there is no `!`

The behaviour changes the issue is about were released as breaking in #1163:
- TS, Go and Dart now accept an old `issuedAt` when a later `expiresAt` is stated.
- They clamp, and so in effect refuse, an `expiresAt` more than 30 days after `issuedAt`. Strictly, it is clamped rather than refused at sight: accepted until `issuedAt + 30 d + skew`, then `expired`.

This PR changes no runtime verdict. The vector files and their runners are tests. The Dart HTTPS change adds an optional member to a discovery response. That member describes a window the server already enforces, so a discoverer reads a more accurate window and no document is accepted or refused differently. The one omission (a sub-second horizon) only affects a configuration that was advertising a window wider than it enforced. Under CLAUDE.md's "behavioural breaks count" rule I judge this a `fix` (patch for `trust_tasks_https`), not a break.

## Rust against SPEC §7.2

Rust's `validate_freshness` / `record_expiry` match *Bounding the record*:
- the maximum age applies only where `expiresAt` is absent;
- the record is kept for as long as the document is acceptable;
- the window is half-open at the same instant the record may be dropped.

SPEC names no expiry horizon. A horizon is a consumer choosing to stop accepting before the producer's `expiresAt`, and SPEC leaves the window's values to the consumer (*Acceptance windows*). So the horizon is consistent with SPEC, though "where `expiresAt` is present it fixes both" does not mention it. There is one Rust-side discrepancy, which I did **not** change:

> Rust's `AcceptanceWindow::of_policy` (`trust-tasks-rs/src/discovery.rs`) drops a horizon that rounds below one second (`NonZeroU64::new` → `None`) but still advertises the window. A `FreshnessPolicy` with a zero or sub-second `expiry_horizon` therefore advertises "the maximum age applies to every document". That is wider than the clamp-at-`issuedAt` it enforces for any document with an `expiresAt`, which breaks discovery responder rule 1. It is an edge configuration (the default horizon is 30 days). The Dart server in this PR omits the window instead. I left Rust unchanged here.

## Checks run locally
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --no-default-features --features acl --test freshness_vectors`: 2/2. `cargo fmt --all -- --check` and `cargo clippy … --test freshness_vectors -- -D warnings` are clean.
- `trust-tasks-ts`: `npm test` 248/248.
- `trust-tasks-go`: `gofmt -l .` (empty), `go vet ./...`, `go test ./...`: all pass.
- `trust-tasks-dart`: `dart test` (270), `dart analyze --fatal-infos`, and `dart format` at the floor language version: clean.
- `trust-tasks-dart-https`: `dart test` (86), `dart analyze --fatal-infos`, and `dart format` at the floor: clean.

Not run locally: the full Rust workspace tests (left to CI).

title: fix(ts,go,dart,rs): whole-second capability-client issuedAt, tested Dart core floors, TS default export condition, Go schema caching
body:
Fixes from the 2026-11-11 repo-wide review across the TypeScript, Go and Dart packages, plus one small Rust discovery fix. No public API break, so there is no `!`.

Closes #1114
Closes #1115
Closes #1108
Part of #1119 (the doc/comment items and the parked `Proof.created` item remain)
Part of #1110 (the consumer consolidation remains, parked)
Part of #1112 (the module split remains, parked)

## Per issue

### #1114: capability clients stamp `issuedAt` at full precision. Fully addressed.
- **Dart** `trust_tasks_capability_client` stamped with `toIso8601String()` (microseconds). It now stamps through the core's `systemClock()` (whole seconds, UTC), and a new test pins this for `buildDocument` and `newAttempt`.
- **Go** `capabilityclient` already wrote whole seconds through `time.RFC3339`. It now uses `trusttasks.SystemClock`, which the required core `v0.10.23` already has, and gains a test.
- **TS** `-capability-client` already stamped whole seconds and already had a test (`wholeSecondsNow`, written out on purpose so it works with every core its peer range admits). No change.
- Not done: the optional repo-wide lint for `toIso8601String()` / `toISOString()` / `time.Now()` flowing into document fields.

### #1115: Dart sibling `trust_tasks` floors. Fully addressed.
Each floor was found by checking the published cores: drop the override, pin `^X`, run `dart pub downgrade`, then `dart analyze lib example`. pub.dev has 0.9.3–0.9.10 and 0.9.23–0.9.37. Versions 0.9.11–0.9.22 never published.
| package | was | now | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `trust_tasks_https` | ^0.9.3 | **^0.9.23** | `lib/` imports `trust_task_discovery/v0_4` |
| `trust_tasks_didcomm` | ^0.9.3 | **^0.9.23** | the example imports `v0_4`; `lib/` needs 0.9.6 (`received:`) |
| `trust_tasks_tsp` | ^0.9.3 | **^0.9.23** | same as didcomm |
| `trust_tasks_proof` | ^0.9.3 | **^0.9.6** | the example passes `received:` |
| `trust_tasks_capability_client` | ^0.9.3 | ^0.9.3 | still compiles there |

- `dart.yml` `packages` job: adds one `downgrade` leg per sibling on stable. Each leg removes only the `trust_tasks` override (tsp keeps its `affinidi_tsp` git override), runs `dart pub downgrade`, then `dart analyze --fatal-infos lib [example]`. `test/` is left out because it may use in-tree core API that the floor predates. If the floor names a core that is not on pub.dev yet, the leg **warns and skips**. That happens on a Release PR crossing a minor (`raise-dart-core-floor.mjs`) or a PR that adds core API and its first use together. Without the skip, it would contradict the Release PR's floor raising. I simulated all five legs locally and they pass. `actionlint` is clean.
- RELEASING.md: one paragraph next to the existing floor-raise text. The Release PR owns the upper end, a feature PR owns the lower end, and the downgrade leg checks it.
- `check-sibling-core-ranges`, `check-dart-packages` and `scripts/test-release/*.test.mjs` all pass.
- TS siblings (`-proof`, `-tsp`, `-capability-client`, all `^0.28.0`): each builds and passes its tests against `@openvtc/trust-tasks@0.28.0` installed in place of the in-tree core. Left unchanged.

### #1119: Dart code items. Part of #1119.
- `HttpsServer.handle` really never throws now. Encoding the reply (the caller's `encodeResponse`, then `jsonEncode`) runs inside a try and becomes `internalError`/500. `handle` also has a last-resort catch around the whole pipeline. Tests cover an encoder that throws and one that returns something `jsonEncode` cannot write.
- `consume.dart`: **already fixed on main** by #1177 (`settleEncoding` settles the claim when the response encoder throws, with a test in `replay_test.dart`). No change.
- Generator `_replaceOutput`: copies into a temporary directory next to the output, then swaps it in by renames. The old tree is renamed aside and deleted only after the new one is in place, and it is restored if the second rename fails. The output path is normalized first (`.`, `..`, trailing separator). A test checks that no sibling directory is left behind for three spellings of the path.
- `trust-tasks-dart-capability-client/example/main.dart` added. It runs.
- **Left for the other PR / parked:** the documentation and comment items (the `0.5`/`0.6` comment, the `release-dart-pr.sh` name, the README/example teaching `acl/grant/v0_2`, the canonical.dart claim) are handled separately. **`Proof.created` optionality is parked** as a cross-language design decision.

### #1110: Go UUID generators. Part of #1110.
- `didcomm/envelope.go` and `capabilityclient/capabilityclient.go` ignored `crypto/rand.Read` errors, which would mint an all-zero id. They now panic, as `tsp`'s `NewURNUUID` already did.
- **Parked:** consolidating the tsp/didcomm consumers into the core (and their divergence on an unparsable body), plus a core `NewURNUUID`. Nested modules require a *published* core, so a new core API cannot be used in the same PR anyway.

### #1112: Go performance and determinism. Part of #1112.
- `trusttasks/extends.go`: payload schemas are parsed once (cached in a `sync.Map` keyed by the schema text, not the Type URI, so two policies with the same URI and different schemas cannot collide). Compiled `patternProperties` regexes are cached too. Patterns are tried in **sorted** order, so when two matching patterns have different subschemas the choice is deterministic. New internal tests cover this.
- `proof/jcs.go`: each member name is encoded to UTF-16 once, outside the sort comparator. The byte-for-byte `eddsa-jcs-2022` fixture test still passes, and a new test orders an astral-plane key before a U+F000 key through `canonicalize`.
- **Parked:** the runtime/generated-tree module split.

### #1108: TS `exports` and `engines`. Fully addressed.
- In `trust-tasks-ts`, `-proof`, `-tsp`, `-capability-client` and `-gen`, every `exports` entry is now `types` first, then **`default`** (replacing `import`, which `default` still matches). The core's `npm run smoke` now resolves `@openvtc/trust-tasks/runtime` by package name through both `import()` and `require()`. The `require()` case is the one that used to fail with `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED`.
- `engines.node: ">=20.19.0"` in all five (`-gen` was `>=20`). Reasons: `@noble/curves` and `@noble/hashes` 2 declare `>= 20.19.0` (proof and tsp depend on them), and 20.19 is the first 20.x that can `require()` ESM, which is what the `default` condition is for. The code itself targets ES2022 and needs the global Web Crypto API (Node 19+). The repo's own tooling floor (`>=24` in the root `package.json`) is a separate thing and unchanged. Each README states the floor and, where it applies, the secure-context requirement for `crypto.randomUUID` in browsers.
- Not done: aligning the compiler majors (the core uses TS 6, the siblings TS 5). The TS-5 siblings build against the core's TS-6 declarations here and in the floor check above.
- api-extractor only compares `.d.ts`, which this does not change. `scripts/api-compat.test.mjs` passes.

### Extra (from the coordinator): Rust `AcceptanceWindow::of_policy`
A zero, sub-second or negative `expiry_horizon` was dropped while the window was still advertised. That reads as "max age applies to every document", which is wider than what is enforced (discovery responder rule 1). Now no window is advertised in that case, matching the Dart HTTPS server. Test: `a_sub_second_expiry_horizon_advertises_no_window`.

## Verified locally
- TS: `npm ci && npm run build && npm test` in all five packages (core 212, proof 89, tsp 14, capability-client 18, gen 30), plus `npm run smoke`.
- Go: core `go build/vet/test ./...` and `gofmt -l .` (clean); `tsp`, `didcomm`, `capabilityclient`, `proof` `go vet` + `go test`. Run on Go 1.27; the 1.22 floor was not run locally.
- Dart (3.13.7): `dart analyze --fatal-infos && dart test` in the core and all five siblings; formatting checked at each package's floor language version. The 3.3/3.6/3.8 SDK floors were not run locally.
- Rust: `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --no-default-features --features acl --lib discovery`, plus clippy `-D warnings` for that feature set. The full workspace was not built.
