title: trust-tasks-https-v0.40.0
body:
### Build & CI

- **https**: Jsonwebtoken 11 in trust-tasks-https, jsonschema 0.60 in trust-tasks-rs ([#1290](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1290))

Aligns the two dependencies a downstream workspace (OpenVTC VTI) compiles
  twice because these crates pinned older majors: jsonschema 0.49 in
  trust-tasks-rs (`validate` feature) beside its 0.60, and jsonwebtoken 10 in
  trust-tasks-https (`jwt` feature) beside its 11.

  jsonschema is private to trust-tasks-rs (no jsonschema type is in its public
  API) and needed no code change. jsonwebtoken is public through
  `JwtBearerAuth::new(DecodingKey, Validation, _)`, so a consumer that builds
  those values with jsonwebtoken 10 must move to 11: a break of the `jwt`
  feature's API, hence the `!`. No source change was needed in this crate.



### Fixed

- **rs,https,ts,go,dart**: Refuse a document that marks an unrecognized ext namespace critical ([#1256](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1256))

* fix(rs,https,ts,go,dart)!: refuse a document that marks an unrecognized ext namespace critical

  SPEC §4.5.2 rule 4: a consumer that does not recognize a namespace named in
  extCritical MUST NOT process the document and MUST reject it with
  unsupportedExtension. No runtime read the member, so a document whose payload
  type does not model it was processed as if the namespace were absent.

  Each runtime gains a check (check_critical_extensions, checkCriticalExtensions,
  CheckCriticalExtensions) that walks the payload as received alongside its
  schema, applies rules 1, 2 and 4, and runs in every consume pipeline after
  the proof and per-specification checks and before the item-11 record. The
  recognized namespaces are a new consume-checks option, empty by default.
  Shared vectors in fixtures/consume/ext-critical.json pin the four together.

title: fix(rs,ts,go,dart): issue an error response as the consumer, not as the rejected document's recipient
body:
SPEC §8.1: "The *error response*'s `issuer` is the *consumer* that emitted it." All four runtimes built the error with `issuer: request.recipient`. That is the rejected document's in-band `recipient`, which is wrong in two cases:

- **Refusals raised before §7.2 item 5.** An expired, malformed, unsupported-type or similar document has not had its `recipient` checked, so the error claimed whatever issuer the sender wrote.
- **`wrongRecipient`.** The in-band `recipient` is by definition a party this consumer is not, yet the refusal claimed to be issued by that party.

Example: an authenticated HTTPS caller posting `"recipient": "did:web:bank.example"` to a server whose `localVid` is `did:web:svc.example` got back a `wrongRecipient` error with `"issuer": "did:web:bank.example"`.

## Was it intended?

No. §8.1 states the rule without qualification, and none of the runtimes' docs describe another intent. Success responses are unaffected: `respond_with` also uses `request.recipient`, but only after item 5 has established that it is this consumer or absent. The spec gives no rule for a consumer that does not know its own identity. That case is handled below by leaving the issuer out, which §4.8.1 allows, since a transport-derived identity supplies it.

## What changed (all four runtimes, the transport-level `reject` only)

`TransportHandler::reject` (Rust), `reject` (TS), `Reject` (Go) and `reject` (Dart) now set the error's `issuer` as follows:

- to the transport's own identity (`derive_parties().recipient` / `deriveParties().recipient` / `DeriveParties().Recipient`) where the transport has one. This is the HTTPS server's `localVid`, the TSP/DIDComm recipient, and so on;
- with no transport identity, to the in-band `recipient` as before, **except** under `wrongRecipient`, where the `issuer` is left out.

`reject_with`, `reject_with_recipient`, `rejectWith`, `rejectWithRecipient`, `RejectWithRecipient` and `rejectWithRecipient` are unchanged. These are the builders a handler uses when it refuses after the pipeline has validated the recipient. Every pipeline refusal (`consume_inbound` / `consumeInbound`, the HTTPS servers, the TSP and DIDComm consumers) goes through the transport-level `reject`. The Rust `GuardedConsumer`'s refusal of an unparsable body already issued as the transport's identity.

## Behaviour changes (R3.6)

- Error responses built by the pipelines carry the transport's own identity as `issuer`. For a document whose `recipient` named this consumer, which is every case a conforming producer sends, the value is unchanged.
- `wrongRecipient` and pre-item-5 refusals no longer echo the sender-chosen `recipient` as `issuer`.
- With a transport that has no identity of its own (`UnauthenticatedTransport`, `InMemoryHandler::new()`), a `wrongRecipient` error has no `issuer`.
- A client that checks an error response's `issuer` against the VID it addressed (for example `HttpsClient` with `server_vid` set) now sees the server's real identity on a misaddressed request. Before, it saw the identity it had addressed.
- No signature changes, so this is not marked `!`.

## Tests

Each runtime gains the same case:

- with a transport identity, both `wrongRecipient` and `proofRequired` on a misaddressed document are issued as that identity;
- without one, `wrongRecipient` carries no `issuer`, and `proofRequired` on a correctly addressed document keeps the in-band recipient.

The tests are `trust-tasks-rs/tests/error_flow.rs` `handler_reject_issues_the_error_as_the_consumer`, the TS `consume.test.ts` block "§8.1 — the error response is issued by the consumer", Go `TestRejectIssuesTheErrorAsTheConsumer`, and the Dart `consume_test.dart` group of the same name.

Only `cargo fmt`, `gofmt` and `dart format` were run locally. CI runs the tests.

## Checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): n/a
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1): n/a
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4): n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*): no type changed; the value of `issuer` on pipeline error responses changes as listed (R3.6); all four runtimes changed together
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*): with no transport identity, nothing unverified is claimed under `wrongRecipient`
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*): an error no longer names an issuer the consumer has not established
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): no mutations
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers: none

title: feat(rs,build): a generated file names the runtime contract it needs
body:
This adds a generator/runtime compatibility marker, option (a) of the decision brief for #1101.

- **Runtime item.** `trust-tasks-rs` gains `#[doc(hidden)] pub const __private::ABI_V1: () = ();`. Its doc says when to add `ABI_V2`.
- **Generated reference.** Every file `trust-tasks-build` generates for an application (`generate_locked`, the `build.rs` path) opens with `const _: () = ::trust_tasks_rs::__private::ABI_V1;`. The comment above it names the `trust-tasks-build` version and says what an unresolved `ABI_V1` means. If the runtime is too old for the generator, or has moved to a newer contract, the build fails on that line with an error naming the contract, not inside some hidden door deep in an `include!`d file.
- **Through a facade.** `Target::with_runtime(path)` (for example the `trust-tasks` facade) emits `{path}::__private::ABI_V1`. The facade's `pub use trust_tasks_rs::*` already re-exports it.
- **Prebuilt tree unchanged.** The in-repo prebuilt tree (`Target::runtime_crate`) does not emit the marker, so nothing regenerates.
- **Not covered.** A caller of `generate_module` alone gets no marker. That function returns one module, not a file.
- **Docs.** The `trust-tasks-build` README explains the line.
- **Release.** Additive for both crates. No version bump in this PR.

Not done here: the brief's optional CI leg that builds `examples/consumer-app` against the last *published* `trust-tasks-rs`. It is a separate workflow change, and that build will only become meaningful once a release carrying `ABI_V1` is published.

Checked locally: `cargo test -p trust-tasks-build --all-features` (a new assertion pins exactly one marker line), `cargo run` / `cargo test -p trust-tasks-example-consumer-app` (the generated file carries the line and compiles), and `cargo clippy -p trust-tasks-build -p trust-tasks-rs --all-targets -D warnings`.

Closes #1101

title: feat(rs,https)!: build the HTTPS server on consume_dispatched; async handlers and auth
body:
The Rust HTTPS server ran its own copy of the §7.2 pipeline, and that copy had drifted from `consume_core` on routing, item 2 and check order (#1089). Its handlers and `Auth::resolve` were synchronous and ran on the async executor (#1090). This PR rebuilds `HttpsServer` on the shared pipeline and adds async handlers and async authentication.

## What changes

**One pipeline.** The server now keeps only what is HTTP: the body limit, the content type, the bearer token and the mapping of an outcome onto a status line. Every framework check runs in `trust_tasks_rs::consume_dispatched_answer` over an `AsyncDispatcher`. Proofs are verified over the body as received (`ProofPolicy::VerifyReceived`, or `RejectIfPresentReceived` with no verifier). The item-11 digest is taken over the received body too, as before.

**trust-tasks-rs additions:**
- `consume_dispatched_answer` and `AnswerOutcome<A>`. This is `consume_dispatched` for a dispatcher whose handlers answer with any `Serialize`. The server's handlers answer `Option<Value>`, where `None` is a fire-and-forget acknowledgement. An answer that serialises to `null` is recorded as "no response", so a duplicate of an acknowledged document is still absorbed in silence (204). `consume_dispatched` is now a thin wrapper over it, and `consume_inbound` is unchanged in shape.
- The checks only the server had are now `ConsumeChecks` options, so every binding can use them:
  - `require_attribution`
  - `proof_did_methods`: the DID-method pre-screen, which runs before the proof policy.
  - `received_bytes` and `default_max_document_bytes`: the per-type `maxDocumentBytes` bound. `consume_inbound` and `consume_dispatched` apply it as soon as the type is known.
- The "identity first when no sender is authenticated" order (§8.1 suppression) is now part of `consume_core` itself. It only differs when the transport reports a recipient but no sender, which is the HTTPS case. The message bindings always authenticate a sender, so they are unaffected.
- `impl ProofVerifier for dyn DynProofVerifier`, so an erased verifier can be handed to `ProofPolicy`.
- `RouteFacts` now carries `MAX_DOCUMENT_BYTES`.

**trust-tasks-https additions:**
- `on_async` and `on_ack_async`. Handlers take the typed request and a `RequestContext` by value and return a future.
- `AsyncAuth` (`resolve_async`, boxed future). A blanket `impl<A: Auth> AsyncAuth for A` means every existing `Auth` keeps working, and `with_auth` now takes `impl AsyncAuth`.
- `with_payload_validator`, for the item-2 schema residue (#1089).
- `max_body_bytes` and `HttpsServer::body_limit()`.

**Includes #1117 (the Rust HTTPS half) and #1121 (the Rust HTTPS half).** Both fell out of the rebuild:
- A registered slug at an unregistered version is now `unsupportedVersion`. A later version whose `extends` chain reaches a registered one is routed to it, with the payload pruned, and answered as the received version's `#response`.
- The router's body limit is the larger of 256 KiB and the largest `maxDocumentBytes` among the registered request types, unless `max_body_bytes` sets it outright.
- After routing, a document over its own type's bound is `malformedRequest`. A type that declares no bound is held to 256 KiB, or to the explicit `max_body_bytes`.

## Wire behaviour that changes (declared break)

Each item names the document affected and the answer it now gets.

1. A known slug at an unregistered `MAJOR.MINOR` is now `unsupportedVersion` (422) instead of `unsupportedType` (422).
2. A later version declaring `extends` to a registered version is now accepted and served (it was `unsupportedType`).
3. **The payload is parsed before validation.** Before, the payload was deserialized after the claim. Now it is deserialized right after routing, before expiry, freshness, identity, the attribution gate and the proof. A document that fails both a payload parse and one of those checks is now `malformedRequest` instead of that check's code. Two cases matter:
   - An unauthenticated, proofless document with a bad payload gets `malformedRequest`, not `proofRequired`.
   - A conflicting resend under a reused `id` with a bad payload gets `malformedRequest`, not `idConflict`.

   `end_to_end.rs` `different_document_under_a_reused_id_is_an_id_conflict` used a member `acl/list/0.3` does not define (`pageSize`) as its "different content". I changed it to a valid `role` filter. The test's intent is unchanged.
4. **Per-spec policy now runs before the claim.** The policy covers `recipient` REQUIRED, `proof` REQUIRED, audience binding and `issuedAt` REQUIRED. It used to run after the claim, inside the dispatch closure, with the claim released on refusal. It now runs before the claim, as `consume_core` does. So a policy-violating document under an `id` that is already recorded is now refused on policy grounds instead of being answered as a duplicate or `idConflict`.
5. **A handler's non-retryable refusal is now recorded.** Before, the server released the claim on every handler refusal. Now it follows `consume_core`:
   - A **retryable** refusal (`unavailable`, …) releases the claim.
   - A **non-retryable** one (`permissionDenied`, …) is recorded. A bit-for-bit resend is answered with the same error document and its own status (403 again), without running the handler.

   A recorded `trust-task-error` replayed as a duplicate keeps its error status rather than 200. `end_to_end.rs` `a_refused_dispatch_releases_the_claim` asserted the old behaviour. It is replaced by `a_retryable_refusal_releases_the_claim` and `a_non_retryable_refusal_is_recorded_and_replayed`. The maintainer confirmed this ("record and replay"). It is `consume_inbound`'s documented semantics (§7.2 "previously determined result"; a new attempt is a new `id`, §8.4), and keeping the old HTTPS behaviour would need a further `ConsumeChecks` option.
6. **Payload-parse messages no longer carry serde detail.** A payload that does not deserialize is `malformedRequest` with `RejectReason::malformed_from_serde`'s category message. This applies to the server and to every `Dispatcher` / `AsyncDispatcher` / `consume_dispatched` caller. The old message was `payload does not match <type>: <serde detail>`, which named the member, the offending value and the offset (§10.4).
7. **Size bounds.** Documents over their type's declared bound, or over 256 KiB for undeclared types under a raised router limit, are `malformedRequest` (400). Documents under a declared bound larger than 256 KiB, previously 413, are accepted.
8. **The claim is keyed per issuer.** The item-11 claim is made with `claim_for(resolved issuer, …)` instead of `claim(…)`. The default implementation delegates. `InMemoryReplayGuard` shares capacity per issuer.

Order relative to `docs/runtime-parity.md` and the Dart server:
- The parity doc's `maxDocumentBytes` row is updated, and a row is added for HTTPS `extends` routing.
- `trust-tasks-dart-https` is documented as mirroring this server step for step, and now differs on items 1–5 and 7. CLAUDE.md says so, and that bringing it into line is the Dart half of #1117/#1121 (decision brief group D).

## API changes (why `!`)

- `rs`: `ConsumeChecks` gains public fields, so a struct literal outside the crate now needs `..ConsumeChecks::not_consequential()`. The three binding crates' `checks()` are updated. #1241's `GuardedConsumer` will need the same one-line change when it merges.
- `https`:
  - `with_auth` takes `impl AsyncAuth`. Source-compatible for every `Auth`.
  - `on` and `on_ack` require `P: Send`, which every generated payload is.
  - `MAX_BODY_BYTES` is unchanged in value. It is now documented as the floor and default bound.

## Handlers and blocking: `block_in_place`, not `spawn_blocking`

The brief suggested `spawn_blocking` for sync handlers. I used `tokio::task::block_in_place` on a multi-threaded runtime (inline on a current-thread one) instead, and documented why. With `spawn_blocking`, a request abandoned by `TimeoutLayer` or by a disconnect releases its item-11 claim while the closure keeps running on the blocking pool. A resend could then execute the effect a second time concurrently with the first. `block_in_place` frees the worker's other tasks without making the handler outlive its request.

The documented consequence: `request_timeout` bounds async handlers, not sync ones. Async handlers are cancelled at an await point, and their claim is released, as `consume_core` already documents. `tokio` gains its `rt-multi-thread` feature in this crate.

## Security review

- **Auth before handler.** The bearer token is resolved before the pipeline. The attribution gate (`require_attribution`, still on by default) runs after identity and before the proof and the handler, in the same place as before.
- **Error routing to the authenticated party.** Pipeline refusals go through `HttpsHandler::reject` (§8.1). Handler refusals are routed the same way, from a header copy of the request. A suppressed answer is still the generic `malformedRequest`/400.
- **Body limit before buffering.** `DefaultBodyLimit` still applies before the body is read. It only grows as far as a registered task's own declaration, so a server that registers no large task never buffers more than 256 KiB.
- **DID-method pre-screen.** The screen and its default (`did:key` only with a verifier) are unchanged and still run before the verifier. The proof is still the last step that can egress before the claim.
- **New exposure.** Payload deserialization now precedes the attribution gate, so an unauthenticated stranger learns "payload malformed" for a supported type. The message is category-only now (item 6), and routing already revealed that the type is supported.
- **Replayed refusals.** A replayed non-retryable refusal is returned to whoever resends the identical document. That is the same exposure the server already had for recorded success responses: identity and attribution still run before the record is consulted.

## Cancellation mid-handler (security review follow-up)

Before, cancelling a request while its async handler ran (timeout, disconnect, RST_STREAM) released the item-11 claim through `HeldClaim::drop` → `release_abandoned`. An effect that had already committed could then execute again on a resend.

Now, once the handler has started, cancellation leaves the claim **in flight**:
- A resend is answered as an in-flight duplicate (`202` over HTTPS) until the record expires with the acceptance window. It is never re-executed.
- Cancellation before the handler first runs still releases the claim, as does cancellation after it returns (during a retryable refusal's release). A handler panic still releases it too.

This is a `consume_core` change, so it applies to every Rust binding. `trust-tasks-rs/tests/replay_guard.rs` `a_cancelled_handler_releases_the_claim_so_a_resend_runs` asserted the old behaviour; it is now `a_handler_cancelled_after_committing_is_not_executed_again`. A new HTTPS test, `an_async_handler_cancelled_after_committing_is_not_executed_again`, covers a 408 followed by a resend that gets 202 with no second execution.

`block_in_place` stays for sync handlers. `spawn_blocking` would no longer double-execute, but it would run on with nobody left to record its result.

## Tests

- New `trust-tasks-https/tests/pipeline.rs` (13 tests) uses hand-written `example.test` payload types. It covers async handlers, async refusal routing, async ack plus a silent duplicate, `AsyncAuth`, a blocking sync handler on a multi-thread runtime, `extends` routing, `unsupportedVersion` vs `unsupportedType`, the derived and overridden body limit, declared and default per-type bounds, 413, and the payload validator.

title: ci: pin the Rust toolchain, build PRs from the committed SPEC.md, and add SECURITY.md
body:
This PR groups four repository and CI hygiene items.

Rust toolchain (#1142). A root rust-toolchain.toml pins Rust 1.100.0, the stable that dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable resolves to in CI today (released 2026-11-09), with the rustfmt and clippy components. Every job that used dtolnay/rust-toolchain with `toolchain: stable` (twenty steps across eight workflows) now uses a small composite action, .github/actions/rust-toolchain. The action installs the toolchain the file names, makes it the default, and keeps the environment variables the dtolnay action set. rust.yml's path filter now includes the file and the action. There is no MSRV job in the workspace today. The note in rust.yml that explains why now also says that any future MSRV job must select 1.95 with RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN, because the file overrides `rustup default`. A new weekly workflow, rust-toolchain-bump.yml, reads the current stable from static.rust-lang.org. When that stable is newer than the pin, the workflow opens or refreshes one signed-off PR titled "ci: build with Rust <version>". It follows withdraw.yml's pattern: it authors the commit as the token owner and uses RELEASE_PLZ_TOKEN so the PR's CI runs. A new root .npmrc sets engine-strict=true. npm reads it only for installs at the repository root, so the published packages, each in its own directory, are unaffected. The root `engines.node` (>=24) already matched .nvmrc (24).

SPEC.md on pull requests (#1138). generate-framework-spec.mjs gains a `--check-committed` mode, also available as `npm run check-framework-spec`. It reads the canonical commit that SPEC.md's banner names, regenerates from that commit, and fails only when the committed file differs from that output, for example after a hand edit or a legacy-anchors change that was never regenerated. Its answer does not change when canonical main moves. deploy.yml runs this check on pull requests instead of regenerating from canonical main. Pushes to main, the nightly schedule and repository_dispatch still regenerate from canonical main, so the site keeps serving the latest canonical text. A new report-failure job runs when a scheduled or dispatched run fails. It opens an issue titled "Scheduled website deploy is failing", or comments on the open one, using GITHUB_TOKEN with `issues: write`.

SECURITY.md (part of #1125). Vulnerabilities are reported through GitHub private vulnerability reporting. Fixes go into the latest release of each package, listed for crates.io, npm, Go and pub.dev, and the file notes that Go tags cannot be withdrawn, so Go fixes go forward with `retract`. None of the 121 trustoverip repositories has a SECURITY.md (each was checked through the contents API), and the org-level .github repository has none to inherit, so there is no ToIP-mandated channel to follow. The PR template and code-of-conduct link from #1125 are not in this PR.

A maintainer must enable private vulnerability reporting by hand. It is currently off for this repository (`{"enabled": false}`): Settings, then Code security, then Private vulnerability reporting. Until it is enabled, the link in SECURITY.md has no form behind it.

CODEOWNERS (#1144). No second owner exists, so the text changes to say so. CODEOWNERS's header, CLAUDE.md, CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md and README.md no longer say that CODEOWNERS routes review per namespace or requires several approvals. The website no longer derives a spec's displayed authors from CODEOWNERS, which credited about 38 families to one handle. build-registry.mjs now uses front-matter authors first and the spec folder's git history next, skipping `[bot]` authors. The "(CODEOWNERS)" label on the spec page is removed, and new-spec.mjs's template comment changes to match. Adding a second owner or a maintainers team for the release-critical paths is a people decision and is not part of this PR.

Checked: actionlint on every workflow, `npm run check`, `npm run test:checks`, `npm run test:website`, and `--check-committed` against both the committed SPEC.md (passes) and a modified copy (fails).

title: fix(ts-gen,go): write bundle text into generated code only as data
body:
The consumer-side generators turn a vendored registry bundle into source code. A generated module should be a function of the bundle's schema *data*: no bundle string should be able to end a comment or add a declaration. Four places in `trust-tasks-gen-ts` wrote bundle text into the module without holding it to a grammar first:

- **The banner comment** carries the bundle's `typeUri`. `parseBundle` only checked that it was a string, so a value containing `*/` ended the comment.
- **`@deprecated` doc comments** carry the bundle's `deprecation`, which was also only checked to be a string.
- **json-schema-to-typescript reads `tsType` and `tsEnumNames` as TypeScript source.** The generator adds `tsType` itself to name hoisted definitions. Nothing stopped a bundle schema from arriving with one already set, and the compiler emits its value verbatim.
- **Schema constants are emitted as `JSON.stringify(...)` object literals.** A `"__proto__"` member in such a literal sets the object's prototype instead of defining the member, so the emitted constant silently differs from the schema.

A shared definition with no `title` was also named from its `defOrigins` entry, and that name went into `tsType` and the import/export clauses unchecked.

The Go `trust-tasks-gen` writes `deprecation` into a `// Deprecated:` line, so a note containing a line break would have started a line of Go. Dart (`dartString`, `@Deprecated(...)`) and Rust (`syn`/`quote` literals) already escape both values. Go's banner uses only lock-validated slug, version and digest.

## What changed

`trust-tasks-ts-gen`:

- `parseBundle` (and `generateModule`, for a `Bundle` built by hand) runs the new `checkGeneratedText`, which refuses a bundle when:
  - its `typeUri` is not a bare SPEC §6.1 Type URI (path form `<prefix>/spec/<slug>/<M.N>` or URN form, not `http`), or its prefix holds a character outside the RFC 3986 set (`*` is excluded too);
  - its `deprecation` is not exactly `retired`, `retired; use <slug>/<M.N>` or `superseded by <slug>/<M.N>`, the notes `trust-tasks-build` writes and `check-bindings` compares;
  - any subschema of `schema` or `responseSchema` carries `tsType` or `tsEnumNames`. The walk is keyword-aware, so a payload member *named* `tsType` is still accepted;
  - any object in either schema has a member named `__proto__`.
- The banner line is asserted free of `*/` and line terminators before it is written.
- `buildComponentRegistry` refuses a shared-definition name that is not a TypeScript identifier.

`trust-tasks-go/cmd/trust-tasks-gen`: refuses a bundle whose `deprecation` is not one of the same three notes.

Registry build: `scripts/lib/generator-keywords.mjs` finds `tsType` / `tsEnumNames` in a schema. `build-registry.mjs` fails on any payload or shared schema under `specs/` that carries one, so the registry cannot publish one either. No spec carries one today.

## Behaviour changes (R3.6)

- `trust-tasks-gen-ts` and the Go `trust-tasks-gen` refuse bundles they used to accept, as listed above. Every bundle the registry builds today passes: all 331 deprecation notes and every request Type URI in the prebuilt TypeScript modules match the new grammars. The test fixtures' Type URIs (`https://…`, `did:web:…/spec/…`, `urn:…:spec:…`) are accepted.
- `npm run build` fails on a spec schema carrying `tsType` or `tsEnumNames`.
- Generated output for an accepted bundle is byte-for-byte unchanged.
- No signature changed; the new helpers are additions in `bundle.ts`, not exported from the package root. Not marked `!`.

## Tests

- `trust-tasks-ts-gen/test/generate.test.ts`, "bundle text reaches a module only as data":
  - generator keywords are refused in a property, a definition, the response schema and a `oneOf` branch, while a member named `tsType` is still accepted;
  - `__proto__` is refused under `properties` and inside a `const`;
  - malformed Type URIs are refused, including ones that would close the banner comment or add a line, and the three accepted forms pass;
  - deprecation notes are checked the same way;
  - `generateModule` checks a bundle it was handed directly;
  - a shared definition whose name would not be an identifier is refused.
- `trust-tasks-go/cmd/trust-tasks-gen/gen_test.go` `TestRefusesADeprecationThatIsNotALifecycleNote`.
- `scripts/test-checks/generator-keywords.test.mjs` (run by `npm run test:checks`).

Only formatters (`gofmt`) were run locally. CI runs the tests.

## Checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): n/a
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1): n/a; generation still writes nothing when a bundle is refused
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4): n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*): no wire type changed; the bundle format is unchanged and is now read more strictly (R3.6 above)
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*): unrecognised bundle text is refused, not passed through
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*): each refusal names the member and the grammar it failed
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): no mutations
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers: none

title: ci(specs): promote only the latest version, track the current framework, ratchet missing descriptions
body:
This adds the three lints from the #1132 decision brief. It runs no batch promotion and re-targets no specs.

## 1. Promotion rule: only the latest version of a slug is promoted

"Superseded" is computed from maturity: a later live version at an equal or higher maturity supersedes an earlier one. Promoting an **older** version above a newer `draft` would therefore make it current again. All four generators would drop its deprecation, and its withdrawal date would move.

The new `npm run check-spec-lifecycle` (`scripts/check-spec-lifecycle.mjs`) refuses a PR that raises a version's `status` (draft → candidate → standard) when a later live version of the same slug exists. It runs as the `spec lifecycle rules` job in `checks.yml` (PRs only) and in `npm run check`.

The rule is about a *change*, not a state. A newer `draft` published after a promotion is fine, because nothing deprecated becomes current. So the check compares against the merge base, as `check-version-edits` does (working tree vs merge base, so specs not yet committed are checked too). Retiring or withdrawing a version is not a promotion.

The promotion criteria (implementations, a release) and any batch promotion still need the governance decision the brief mentions. This PR only makes sure that, whenever a promotion happens, it cannot cause library churn.

## 2. The current framework version (0.6.0) and the lag rule

`CURRENT_FRAMEWORK_VERSION = '0.6.0'` is defined in `scripts/lib/spec-lifecycle.mjs`. It matches `DEFAULT_FRAMEWORK_VERSION` in `trust-tasks-rs/src/discovery.rs`, and it is the latest release under `specs/_framework/`.

The lag rule:
- **A new version targets the current framework or later.** `check-spec-lifecycle` fails a PR that adds a live version targeting an earlier one, including a version copied from its predecessor.
- **An existing version keeps its target** and moves with its next revision. Nothing is re-targeted in place.

The build checks that the current release is published and equals `DEFAULT_FRAMEWORK_VERSION`, so the two move together. It also reports the lag:

> Framework target: current is 0.6.0; 350 of 851 latest spec version(s) and 5 of 5 binding(s) target an earlier release and move with their next revision

I chose a diff check over the build's git dates because the build reads commit dates. A squash merge stamps the merge date, so a date-based rule would let a PR pass and then fail `main`.

Heads-up: until now, 162 live versions added since 0.6 arrived (2026-09-21) targeted 0.5.0, including some added this week. Open PRs that add a version targeting 0.5.0 will see this job fail once they include this change. The fix is a one-line `targetFrameworkVersion: "0.6.0"`.

## 3. Member-description ratchet

`scripts/lib/member-descriptions.mjs` runs in the build and in `validate`. It counts, in the latest live version of each slug, the payload members with neither a `description` nor a `$ref`.
- The baseline is **897 members in 315 slugs**. The brief's 846 was measured two days earlier; the corpus has grown since.
- The baseline is kept **per slug** in `member-descriptions-baseline.json`, so one slug's fix can't be spent on another slug's regression. A new slug allows none. A new version of an old slug inherits the slug's allowance.
- A slug that exceeds its entry fails the build, and the failure names each member.
- A slug below its entry produces a warning to run `node scripts/lib/member-descriptions.mjs --lower`, which lowers entries and never raises them.

Docs: `CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md` gains "The current framework version" section, the latest-only promotion rule, and the description rule. `CLAUDE.md`'s CI table gains rows for both checks.

## Not done (left on #1132)

- The SPEC.md "Working Draft 0.7.0" vs `_framework/0.6` mismatch. It belongs to the canonical repository.
- The heading-order lint. The brief leaves this to `new-spec`.
- The batch promotion. It waits on the governance decision.

## Verification

- `npm run build` and `npm run check` pass. `check-spec-lifecycle` reports 0 changed spec.md files against the merge base.
- `npm run test:checks` passes 43/43, including 13 new tests in `scripts/test-checks/spec-lifecycle.test.mjs`. They cover the lag rule, promoting the latest vs. an older version, candidate→standard, a newer draft after a promotion, retiring, and the ratchet's fail/pass/lower and latest-only counting.
- `npm run test:website` passes 47/47. `actionlint .github/workflows/checks.yml` is clean.
- Manual check: copying `acl/grant/0.3` to a new `0.9` with a `0.5.0` target, and promoting `acl/grant/0.2` to `candidate`, produced exactly the two expected failures.

Part of #1132.

title: feat(cli): prebuilt trust-tasks binaries on each CLI release, and a no-Rust install path for TS, Go and Dart
body:
TypeScript, Go and Dart developers need the `trust-tasks` CLI to pin and generate tasks, and until now the only way to get it was `cargo install` on Rust 1.95 or later. This change publishes prebuilt binaries with each CLI release and documents how to install without Rust.

How the binaries are triggered: `release-plz release` in publish.yml creates the `trust-tasks-cli-vX.Y.Z` tag and its GitHub Release using `GITHUB_TOKEN`. Events created by that token start no workflow, so a tag or `release: published` trigger would never fire. Instead, the release-plz step now has an id. A following step reads release-plz's `releases` output and picks out the tag for `trust-tasks-cli`, and a new `cli-binaries` job in publish.yml calls the reusable `.github/workflows/cli-binaries.yml` with that tag. On an ordinary merge nothing is released, the tag is empty and the job is skipped. Nothing about the crates.io Trusted Publishing job changes, and publish.yml keeps its name.

cli-binaries.yml checks out the tag and builds `trust-tasks-cli` with `--locked` for x86_64 and aarch64 Linux (on ubuntu-22.04 runners, so the glibc floor is 2.35), aarch64 and x86_64 macOS (x86_64 is cross-compiled on macos-14) and x86_64 Windows (MSVC with a static CRT). Each native build is smoke-tested: `--version` must report the tag's version. The build legs have a read-only token. A separate `upload` job is the only one with `contents: write`, and it compiles nothing. It writes a `.sha256` per archive plus a combined `SHA256SUMS`, and runs `gh release upload --clobber` against the release that release-plz created. If that release does not exist it refuses rather than creating one. The workflow can also be dispatched by hand with a tag, which is how to attach binaries to `trust-tasks-cli-v0.2.0` or retry a failed upload. The tag's own rust-toolchain.toml is used when it has one. v0.2.0 predates that file, so the workflow falls back to stable.

Assets are named `trust-tasks-cli-<version>-<target>.tar.gz` (`.zip` on Windows), with the binary at the archive root. The new `[package.metadata.binstall]` in trust-tasks-cli/Cargo.toml uses the same names, so `cargo binstall trust-tasks-cli` fetches them. This takes effect from the next CLI release, because binstall reads the metadata from the published crate.

Docs: GETTING-STARTED §1 gains "Installing the `trust-tasks` command" (download and verify, `cargo binstall`, `cargo install`) and a "What you bring yourself" table. The table lists the validator, the proof verifier/signer and the transport for each of Rust, TS, Go and Dart, with links to the sibling packages, and states where no transport package exists yet (TS HTTPS and DIDComm, Go HTTPS). The bindings row in §5 now includes `push`. The TS, Go and Dart READMEs each get a short install section and their own row of that table, and the CLI README mentions binstall and the prebuilt archives. RELEASING.md's CLI row describes the new wiring.

No new third-party actions: the workflow uses only the checkout, upload-artifact and download-artifact SHAs already pinned in publish.yml, plus `gh`, `7z`, `tar` and `sha256sum` from the runner images. Build provenance attestations (`actions/attest-build-provenance`) are left out because that action is not in the repo yet. They would be a small follow-up if wanted.

Checked: actionlint, `npm run check` (including `check-release-lists`), `cargo build -p trust-tasks-cli`, and `cargo metadata` showing the binstall table. The workflow itself has not run. The first real run will be the next CLI release, or a manual dispatch for `trust-tasks-cli-v0.2.0`.

The docs half of #1128 (runnable TS/Go/Dart getting-started apps with tested snippets) is not in this PR.

title: fix(rs,https,dart-https): run the attribution gate before the route lookup
body:
Both HTTPS servers, `trust-tasks-https` (Rust) and `trust_tasks_https` (Dart), looked the route up before the attribution gate. A sender with neither a bearer token nor a proof therefore got `unsupportedType` for an unregistered type and `proofRequired` for a registered one. That made the route table readable without attribution, even though discovery keeps it unreadable without authentication. The Dart server also decoded the payload (`malformedRequest`) before the gate, which gave a second way to tell the two apart.

Since #1244 the Rust server runs every framework check through `trust_tasks_rs::consume_dispatched_answer`, and that pipeline routed first. So the Rust part of this change is now made in `trust-tasks-rs`, and applies to every consumer of that pipeline, not only the HTTPS server.

## What changed

The checks that depend on nothing a route holds now run before the route lookup:

1. expiry and recipient, freshness, and identity, in §7.2 order (identity first when there is no authenticated sender, so a misaddressed document is still suppressed per §8.1)
2. the attribution gate
3. the route lookup / type check

The DID-method pre-screen and proof verification still come after the route lookup. So an unregistered `type` still never reaches a resolver, and the existing `unknown_type_is_rejected_before_the_verifier_is_called` test is unchanged.

- Rust core (`trust-tasks-rs/src/consume.rs`): the envelope checks and the attribution gate move out of `consume_core` into a new private `envelope_checks`, which returns the resolved parties. `consume_dispatched_answer` (and so `consume_dispatched` and the guarded consumer) runs it before `dispatcher.route`. `consume_inbound` runs it before its item-3 type check, so the typed and dispatched paths keep the same order. `consume_core` now starts at the payload schema check and takes the resolved parties. Each check still runs once.
- Rust HTTPS (`trust-tasks-https/src/server.rs`): only the module docs change (the pipeline list is renumbered). The server gets the new order from core.
- Dart (`trust-tasks-dart-https/lib/src/server.dart`): the envelope checks and the attribution gate move into `_envelopeChecks`, which runs over the parsed envelope before `_lookup`. `_dispatch` keeps the identity resolution it needs for `RequestContext`. It also keeps the DID-method pre-screen after the payload decode, where it was. `consumeInbound` repeats the pure §7.2 checks as before.

## Behaviour changes (R3.6)

- HTTPS (both servers): a request with no authenticated sender and no proof is refused `proofRequired` (with `requireAttribution` on, the default) whatever its `type`. Before, an unregistered type got `unsupportedType`, another version of a registered specification got `unsupportedVersion`, and an oversized or undecodable payload got `malformedRequest`.
- An unattributed misaddressed document is suppressed, as a registered-type one already was. Before, the route lookup answered first for an unregistered type.
- Every Rust consumer (`consume_inbound`, `consume_dispatched`, `consume_dispatched_answer`, the guarded consumer, and so the TSP and DIDComm bindings): a document that fails both a type-level check (unsupported type or version, size bound, payload parse, payload schema) and an envelope check (expired, stale, wrong recipient, identity mismatch, attribution) is now refused for the envelope check. Documents that fail only one check get the same answer as before.
- Dart: the same ordering for its HTTPS server, as in the previous revision of this PR.
- Authenticated senders, proof-bearing documents and `requireAttribution: false` still get the same answers. A sender attributed only by a proof can still tell registered from unregistered types. Such a sender can already invoke any registered handler, so this PR does not change that.

No public API changes.

## Tests

- Rust `trust-tasks-rs` `consume.rs`: `dispatched_attribution_gate_runs_before_the_route_lookup`. An anonymous sender gets `proofRequired` for both a registered and an unregistered type, and an authenticated sender still gets `unsupportedType`.
- Rust `end_to_end.rs`: `unattributed_sender_gets_one_answer_for_registered_and_unregistered_types`. The same check over HTTP.
- Dart `server_test.dart`: a registered type, its `#response`, an unregistered type, an unregistered version, and an undecodable payload all give `proofRequired` without a token. An authenticated sender still gets `unsupportedType`.

Only `cargo fmt` / `dart format` were run locally. CI runs the tests.

## Checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): no client code
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1): the item-11 claim is still after every refusal
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4): n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*): no wire types changed. The refusal order changed as listed above (R3.6).
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*): the default (`requireAttribution` on) is the configuration that hides the route table
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*): unchanged; refusals emit the same events
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): no mutations moved
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers: none

title: feat(rooms/records/put): 0.6 declares a 2 MiB document bound
body:
`rooms/records/put/0.6` declares the largest request document a host must accept: `maxDocumentBytes.request: 2097152` (2 MiB, the maintainer's choice for #1065).

- **No member changes.** 0.6 `extends: "0.5"`, so a host still implementing 0.5 reads a 0.6 write as a 0.5 one.
- **New version, not an in-place edit.** Adding the bound to the published 0.5 would retroactively narrow what a 0.5 host must accept.
- **Why 2 MiB.** It is the largest body a deployed host (`room-host`) accepts today, so no record either VTI host stores falls outside the bound. A host with a smaller limit, such as `vtc-service` at 64 KiB, must now raise it to conform. Content larger than 2 MiB goes through files, whose chunk tasks declare their own bound.
- **Conformance.** Producer item 1 now states the bound. New host item 18 makes it two-sided: MUST accept up to it, SHOULD refuse above it with `malformedRequest`. `recordTooLarge` stays the code for a smaller per-record limit of a host's own.
- **No response bound.** The response declares none.

Rust, TypeScript, Go and Dart are regenerated. 0.1–0.5 now carry the deprecation note `superseded by rooms/records/put/0.6`. `npm run fix-stale-references` rewrote nothing: references to 0.5 stay current along the `extends` chain.

**Interaction with #1251.** That PR makes the TypeScript and Go generators emit `maxDocumentBytes`. This branch will be merged with `main` again after #1251 lands, and regenerated so that 0.6's TS and Go modules carry the bound.

Checked locally: `npm run check`, `check-bindings` (71 size bounds match Rust and Dart), and the `rooms` conformance tests.

Closes #1065

title: feat(website): response headers policy as code, applied by script and checked against the page
body:
trusttasks.org currently sends no Strict-Transport-Security, Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy or Permissions-Policy header. Its distribution is not managed from this repository, so nothing records what headers it should send. This PR adds the headers as a CloudFront response headers policy kept in the repo, a script that applies it, and checks that keep it in step with the page.

## What changes

- **`infra/cloudfront/response-headers-policy.json`** (new). This is a `ResponseHeadersPolicyConfig` that sets:
  - `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000`. `includeSubDomains` and `preload` are left off until every subdomain is known to serve HTTPS.
  - `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'` plus the three pinned unpkg paths (React 18.3.1, ReactDOM 18.3.1, marked 12.0.2). It also sets `style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'` with Google Fonts, `font-src` for Google Fonts, `img-src 'self' data: https:`, `connect-src 'self'`, `object-src 'none'`, `base-uri 'self'`, `form-action 'self'` and `frame-ancestors 'none'`. There is no `'unsafe-eval'` (the page has had no in-browser compiler since #1257) and no inline script.
  - `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, and a `Permissions-Policy` that turns off camera, microphone, geolocation, payment and the other sensors.
  - The `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` and `Vary: Accept, Accept-Encoding` headers #1152 asks for. A cache behaviour takes only one response headers policy, so these go in the same policy.
- **`infra/cloudfront/apply-response-headers.sh`** (new). It is a dry run by default. With `--apply`, it creates the policy or updates it in place, then attaches it to the default cache behaviour and to every path-pattern behaviour. It refuses to replace a different policy that is already attached. It handles the distribution-config wrapper the same way `associate.sh` does.
- **`infra/cloudfront/verify.sh`** now also checks each header on `/`, on a spec page, and on a negotiated schema.
- **`infra/cloudfront/response-headers.mjs`** (new) turns the policy into a header map. **`scripts/serve-website.mjs`** sends those headers (all except HSTS, which a browser ignores over HTTP). As a result, `npm run smoke:website` in `deploy.yml` loads the built page under the real CSP and fails if the CSP blocks a load.
- **`infra/cloudfront/response-headers-policy.test.mjs`** (new, part of `test:infra`) checks that:
  - every header is set with `Override`;
  - HSTS is at least a year;
  - the CSP has no `'unsafe-eval'` and no inline script, and sets `frame-ancestors 'none'` and `connect-src 'self'`;
  - every `<script src>`, stylesheet and preconnect in `index.template.html` is allowed by the CSP;
  - the template has no inline script or `on…=` handler;
  - every `fetch()` in the page code is same-origin;
  - each `Quantity` matches its list, and the Comment fits CloudFront's limit.
- **`website/index.template.html` / `app.jsx`**: the skip link's inline `onclick` would not run under the CSP, so it moves to a click listener in `app.jsx`. Until the bundle runs, the link is a plain `#main` anchor.
- **Docs**: the infra README's response-headers section (which said "not yet configured") now documents the policy, why each header is there, how to apply it and the IAM actions needed. The CLAUDE.md CI table is updated.

## Behaviour changes (R3.6)

- Nothing changes on the live site until an operator runs `./infra/cloudfront/apply-response-headers.sh <DISTRIBUTION_ID> --apply`. After that the site is no longer framable, and the browser blocks any script, style, font or `fetch` origin the CSP does not list.
- The local dev server (`npm run serve`) now sends the same headers.

## Operator steps after merge

1. `./infra/cloudfront/apply-response-headers.sh <DISTRIBUTION_ID>` to review the dry run, then run it again with `--apply`.
2. Once the distribution shows Deployed, run `./infra/cloudfront/verify.sh`. The header checks are at the end.

## Checklist (development guide §9)

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): N/A, no new client
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): N/A
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1): the apply script is idempotent; it creates or updates the policy before attaching it, and a re-run picks up where a failed run stopped
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4): N/A, no retries; updates use `--if-match`
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): N/A
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): N/A
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*): N/A, HTTP response headers only
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*): the script refuses to replace a policy it did not create
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*): `verify.sh` checks the live headers rather than assuming the apply worked
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): see R2.1 above
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers: none

Refs #1152.

title: site: link-preview and canonical tags, content-hashed page scripts, headless browser smoke test
body:
This makes three website changes.

Link previews and canonical URL (#1151). index.template.html now carries a canonical link, Open Graph tags (site_name, type, url, title, description) and a twitter summary card, all set to the home page's values with the origin https://trusttasks.org. app.jsx rewrites the canonical link, og:url, og:title, og:description and the twitter title and description for each route, next to the existing document.title and meta description logic. The canonical URL ignores registry filters, resolves a versionless spec or binding URL to the version it shows, and keeps the requested path for the not-found view. There is no og:image, because the site has only SVG artwork and link unfurlers expect a raster image. The static per-spec HTML stubs from the issue are still parked.

Content-hashed scripts (#1148). scripts/build-website.mjs now writes a copy of every local script the template loads (markdown.js, routes.js, data.js, tasks.generated.js, ecosystem.js, bindings.js, libraries.js and ceremonies.js) to website/assets/hashed/ as <name>.<sha256-16>.js. The page bundle moves to the same directory, and index.html names the hashed files. The build empties the directory first, so it holds only what the current index.html names. In deploy.yml, assets/hashed/ is uploaded immutable with --size-only before index.html. tasks.generated's copy is still gzip-encoded at rest: it is gzipped into its own directory under the same name, so later syncs compare gzip with gzip and never upload it unencoded. After the new index.html is live, the same two syncs run again with --delete to remove superseded files. The main sync no longer excludes the fixed-name tasks.generated.js or the old assets/app.<hash>.js bundles. The deploy job deletes its local tasks.generated.js first, so that sync's --delete removes those orphaned objects instead of leaving a stale fixed-URL copy. registry.json and /specs/** keep their fixed URLs and cache headers. The stylesheets stay no-cache and unhashed, because style.css imports tokens.css by a relative URL. With this change every item in #1148 is done: the build timestamp, no-cache on pages and the specs max-age landed earlier.

Headless smoke test (#1157). The new npm run smoke:website (scripts/smoke-website.mjs) serves the built site with scripts/serve-website.mjs, which uses the production CloudFront routing function. It loads /, /spec/acl/grant/0.3, /binding/https/0.3, /schema and /implementations/rust in headless Chrome, each in a fresh tab. It fails on an uncaught exception, a console.error, a browser log error, a failed or 4xx/5xx request, a missing h1, the static boot message still showing, the not-found view, or a canonical link other than https://trusttasks.org plus the route. It adds no npm dependency and no action: it drives Chrome over the DevTools protocol using Node's built-in WebSocket. It uses CHROME_PATH or the first Chrome or Chromium on PATH, which is the preinstalled Chrome on CI runners, and passes --no-sandbox under CI. deploy.yml runs it after the build and the website tests. The website-jsx tests now check that the built index.html names a content-hashed, current copy of every template script in order with the bundle last, that assets/hashed/ holds nothing else, and that the link-preview tags are present. The server-side render loads the hashed files that index.html names. CLAUDE.md's CI table has a row for the smoke test.

Verification: npm run build, npm run check, npm run test:website (48 pass), npm run test:infra (33 pass) and actionlint are clean. npm run smoke:website passes all five routes locally against Chrome. With one hashed file deleted it fails every route with the 404, so it catches what it should. The deploy steps cannot be exercised outside main, so the S3 metadata (immutable, gzip encoding) is unverified until the first deploy.

Part of #1151.
Closes #1148.

title: ci(site): generate SPEC.md from a pinned canonical commit, moved by a bump PR
body:
Every deploying run of `deploy.yml` (a push to `main`, the nightly schedule, or a `framework-spec-updated` dispatch) regenerated `SPEC.md` from canonical `main` of trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec and deployed the result. That meant canonical text reached trusttasks.org within a day without any commit or review here; a difference from the committed copy only produced a warning. This PR pins the canonical commit in this repository. The pin moves only through a pull request, and the site serves the committed `SPEC.md`.

## What changes

- **`scripts/framework-spec-source.json`** (new) records the canonical commit (a full SHA) that `SPEC.md` is generated from, plus the ref it was taken from. It starts at `bdf2cdd9256f`, the commit the current `SPEC.md` banner names, so `SPEC.md` itself does not change.
- **`scripts/generate-framework-spec.mjs`**:
  - With no arguments it now generates from the pinned commit, so a local run is reproducible.
  - `--update` (also `npm run bump-framework-spec`) fetches canonical `main`, or `--ref`, then writes both `SPEC.md` and the pin.
  - `--check-committed` regenerates from the pin instead of from the banner.
  - When a full SHA is requested, the script checks that the fetched checkout is that commit and fails otherwise.
  - `--ref` and `--from` still work for local exploration and leave the pin unchanged.
- **`deploy.yml`**:
  - The `schedule` and `repository_dispatch` triggers are removed, along with the step that regenerated from canonical `main`.
  - `npm run check-framework-spec` now runs on every event, not only on pull requests, so a deploy always serves exactly what the pinned commit generates.
  - The failure-issue job moves to the new workflow, since only that workflow is scheduled now.
- **`.github/workflows/framework-spec-bump.yml`** (new) runs nightly at the same cron time, on the `framework-spec-updated` dispatch, and by hand.
  - It runs the generator with `--update`. When the generated text changed, it pushes `framework-spec/bump` and opens or refreshes one PR. The PR body links the canonical compare range, so the change can be reviewed.
  - It is modelled on `rust-toolchain-bump.yml`: it authors commits as the token owner with DCO sign-off, uses `RELEASE_PLZ_TOKEN` so the PR's CI runs, and installs no npm dependencies, because the generator uses Node built-ins only.
  - A failed scheduled or dispatched run opens or comments on a "Framework specification bump is failing" issue.
- **`scripts/test-checks/framework-spec-pin.test.mjs`** (new, part of `test:checks`) checks that:
  - the committed pin is a full SHA, and the `SPEC.md` banner names it;
  - `readPin` rejects short SHAs, branch names and odd refs;
  - `deploy.yml` has no schedule or dispatch trigger, checks the committed copy on every run, and never regenerates from a branch;
  - the bump workflow opens a PR and does not deploy.
- **CLAUDE.md**: the "SPEC.md is generated" section describes the pin and the bump PR.

## Behaviour changes (R3.6)

- A canonical framework change no longer reaches trusttasks.org on its own. It arrives as a "regenerate SPEC.md" PR, and goes live when that PR merges.
- `npm run generate-framework-spec` with no arguments regenerates from the pinned commit instead of from canonical `main`. To move to the latest canonical text, use `npm run bump-framework-spec`.
- The canonical repository's `framework-spec-updated` dispatch now opens the bump PR instead of deploying.

## Checklist (development guide §9)

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): N/A, the fetch is `git fetch` under the job's 10-minute timeout
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): N/A
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1): the bump job force-pushes one fixed branch and refreshes the existing PR, so a re-run picks up where a failed run stopped
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4): N/A, no retries
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): N/A
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): N/A
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*): N/A
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*): a missing or malformed pin fails the check and the deploy; nothing falls back to `main`
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*): a failing scheduled or dispatched bump opens an issue
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): see R2.1 above
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers: none

Follows #1138 and #1250.

title: perf(rs,https): hash, compare and route each inbound document once
body:
Follow-up to #1244 (#1089): the Rust HTTPS server now runs on `consume_dispatched_answer`, so this cuts the repeated work on that inbound path. **No public signature changes**; additions are crate-private.

## Measured first

`trust-tasks-https/examples/inbound_bench.rs` (new, no new dependencies) sends documents through the router as a `tower` service, with no network. Each document has a distinct `id` and goes through the whole §7.2 pipeline: bearer auth, the default replay record and freshness bound, and a trivial handler.

```sh
cargo run --release -p trust-tasks-https --example inbound_bench [filter]
```

Apple Silicon, release build. Best round of 3 alternating A/B runs (7 rounds each); `main` = `origin/main` plus the bench:

| scenario | body | `main` µs/req | this PR µs/req | change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| typical (3 entries) | 628 B | 14.5 | 11.7 | −19% |
| medium (100 entries) | 12.7 KB | 151.7 | 98.6 | −35% |
| large (1500 entries) | 190 KB | 2174 | 1344 | −38% |
| forward route 0.2→0.1, typical | 670 B | 18.4 | 14.4 | −22% |
| forward route 0.2→0.1, medium | 12.8 KB | 187.5 | 131.5 | −30% |
| with payload validator, typical | 628 B | 15.1 | 11.5 | −24% |
| with payload validator, medium | 12.7 KB | 165.3 | 99.5 | −40% |

(The machine was shared and some runs were noisy; the best-of figures were consistent across the three runs.)

## What changed, and what each part bought

Each part was kept only because it was measurably faster on its own:

1. **Item-11 digest streamed into the hasher** (`canonical.rs`). The canonical form is now written straight into an incremental SHA-256, which takes it through a 4 KiB buffer. Before, the code built a `String` of the whole document and then copied it again (`input.to_vec()`) to pad it. String escaping is now written a run at a time instead of a `char` at a time. Digest of the 12.7 KB document: 56 → 40 µs. Writing the tokens into the hasher one at a time with no buffer was barely faster than before (52 µs), so the buffer is needed.
2. **Received-form shortcut on the dispatched path** (`consume.rs`, `is_received_routed_form`). The old check deep-copied `received`, re-read it as `TrustTask<Value>` and serialised both sides to compare them (about 48 µs on medium). Now it first compares `received` with `doc`'s serialisation member by member. `doc`'s headers are serialised with a `()` payload, so the payload is compared in place (pruned along a forward route) and not copied. The shortcut can only say **yes** where the full comparison would. A miss, for example `issuedAt` spelled with an offset or `.000`, falls through to the unchanged full comparison. Unit tests check that the two agree on matches, re-rendered headers, and mismatches.
3. **No second route / prune** (`AsyncDispatcher::dispatch_routed`, `pub(crate)`). `consume_dispatched_answer` already routed and pruned the payload, so it now dispatches to that target directly. Before, `dispatch` routed again and pruned again. Forward route, medium: about 146 → 132 µs (alternating A/B with only this reverted).
4. **The payload validator reads the payload `Value` in place** on the dispatched path. Before, it got `to_value(&Value)`, which is a deep copy. With a validator, medium is now about the same as with no validator, where before it cost about 14 µs more.

## Semantics preserved

- **Proofs** are still verified over `received`, the document as it arrived. Only the cost of deciding that `received` *is* the consumed document changed, and that decision only short-circuits to the answer the full check gives.
- **Item-11 digest bytes are identical.** The new test `replay::tests::digest_values_are_pinned` pins three digests computed on `main` before this change. The documents cover escapes, astral text, every number spelling, unmodelled members, and a document spanning many SHA-256 blocks and the sink's flush point. Tests also check that the incremental hasher matches the one-shot hasher for every split of every length up to 200 bytes, and byte by byte. A further test checks `canonical_sha256_hex(v) == sha256_hex(canonical_json(v))`.
- **§7.2 order is unchanged.** No check moved. `dispatch_routed` runs the same registered handler, including its downcast and `enforce_spec_policy`.

## Considered and not done

- **Parsing the body once.** The server still reads the body twice: once typed and once as a `Value`. Building the typed document from the parsed `Value` (`TrustTask::deserialize(&Value)`, 12.5 µs) instead of reading the bytes a second time (≈20 µs) would save at most about 7% on medium. But the typed read is the one that refuses a duplicated member, and that also applies inside `proof`. Keeping that behaviour exact would need a hand-written `Value` visitor that tracks duplicates and copies how `serde_json` represents numbers under each feature combination (`arbitrary_precision` can be switched on downstream). It would also need the error category to follow the typed read when a body is both mistyped and malformed. I judged that not worth 7%.
- **Carrying the typed payload from the pre-claim check into the handler** (about 5% on medium). `Payload` does not require `Send`, so a type-erased payload cannot be carried across the `await` without a new bound.
- **What dominates now:** the two body parses (~34%) and SHA-256 compression (~30%, ~385 MB/s in software). Hardware SHA-256 (the `sha2` crate, or `aarch64`/SHA-NI intrinsics) would remove most of the second. That is a decision about dependencies and `unsafe` for the core crate, so it is left for a separate PR.
- The `trust-tasks-proof` verifier's document clone (`verify_raw`) is the separate small fix the design brief describes.

## Checks run

`cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --no-default-features --features acl`, `cargo test -p trust-tasks-https -p trust-tasks-didcomm -p trust-tasks-didcomm-v1 -p trust-tasks-tsp -p trust-tasks-proof -p trust-tasks-capability-client`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings` on all of those, `cargo fmt --all --check`, and `cargo doc` (`acl,validate`) with `-D warnings`.

Closes #1092.

title: docs: move the developer guide out of CLAUDE.md
body:
CLAUDE.md had become the only developer guide (#1126). This moves its content into human-facing docs. It is a **move, not a rewrite**: every section is carried verbatim, with only the AI-addressed or self-referential wording adjusted.

## Where everything went

| Old CLAUDE.md section | New home |
|---|---|
| Intro, Build / validate / publish, toolchain pin | `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md` → Repository layout (with a new repo map), Build, validate and regenerate |
| `SPEC.md` is generated | `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md` |
| Category / reserved slug / binding lists, binding-prose paragraph | `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md` → Hand-maintained lists (plus a new entry for `libraries.js`, the fifth list, guarded by `checkLibraryRegistry`) |
| Changing a spec — regenerate; Merging is not releasing; Library versions are semver | `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md` |
| What the CI checks actually assert; generator independence | `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md` |
| Registry bundles, lifecycle, prebuilt deprecation, `extends`, instants, routing consumers, declared error codes, `maxDocumentBytes` | `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md` |
| `#[non_exhaustive]` + builders, `trust-tasks-build`, unit tests see only `acl`, `GuardedConsumer` | `docs/packages/rust.md` |
| Go module + nested modules | `docs/packages/go.md` |
| Hand-written TypeScript packages | `docs/packages/typescript.md` |
| Dart package + hand-written Dart packages | `docs/packages/dart.md` |
| DCO, PR conventions | `CONTRIBUTING.md` |

- **`CONTRIBUTING.md`** is now a contributor guide (DCO, what to run, PR-title rules and the `!` scope rule, no versions/CHANGELOGs, review, where to read more) placed **above the unchanged OWF CLA text**, so the README's "agree to the CLA in CONTRIBUTING.md" stays true.
- **`CLAUDE.md`** is now a short index: the must-not-forget rules as one-line bullets, each linking to its section.
- References into CLAUDE.md by section name were repointed in `deploy.yml`, `GETTING-STARTED.md`, `docs/runtime-parity.md`, `README.md`, `scripts/` comments, `trust-tasks-codegen` (unpublished) and `website/assets/libraries.js`.

## Deliberately not changed

- **References inside published package directories** still say "CLAUDE.md": comments in `trust-tasks-rs/src`, `-ts-gen/src`, the Go `cmd/trust-tasks-gen`, Dart and TS tests, and the Go and Dart READMEs. Editing them would release those packages for a comment change. CLAUDE.md's index still routes those readers to the right section.
- CHANGELOGs, the ADR and the design notes are history, so they are left alone.

## Wording dropped or adjusted

Every non-empty line of the old file was compared against the new docs. The only lines not carried over word for word are these:

- "The part of this file that most recently changed. If you have a recollection…": reworded for a human reader. The warning that the old flow is gone stays.
- "see below", "the table above", "the callout above", "the callout at the top of this file", and "see 'Consumers that route on the Type URI'" became links to the new sections. "the `data.js` trap below" became "above", because the order changed.
- PR conventions: the bullet "DCO sign-off is mandatory… see the callout" is dropped. It repeated the DCO section, which now sits in the same file.
- go.md: "the call the user made" became "the call the maintainers made".
- The prebuilt-deprecation section had a misplaced sentence. "The TS, Go and Dart equivalence tests mask exactly the mark…" had been spliced after the #1102 paragraph, so it was moved back to the paragraph it belongs to.

## Follow-ups (not in this PR)

- The CI-check table still omits the 12 `build-registry.mjs` checks that #1126 lists (`checkProofFloor` … `checkCommittedRecordMirror`). Adding them is new content, not part of the move.

`npm run check` and `npm run build` pass. The relative links and `#anchors` in the new and edited docs were checked against GitHub's slug rules.

Closes #1126.

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.40.0
body:
### Added

- **messaging**: Wake a device through its own mediator, and end-to-end delivery receipts ([#1297](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1297))

Two gaps in getting a document to a device that is on another mediator
  or has no agent of its own.

  Waking (messaging/wake/set 0.1, messaging/wake/request 0.1):
  - messaging/wake/set: an account gives its own mediator the opaque
    WakeHandle its push gateway issued, or clears it (absent = clear). The
    mediator never holds a token. Response { wakeCapable }.
  - messaging/wake/request: a sender that has just queued mail for a DID
    asks that DID's mediator to ring, naming the queued messages by their
    stored ids (<= 8). Contentless. The mediator rings (push/wake, as
    itself) only when the account has a handle, every id is queued for it,
    fresh (10 min) and undelivered, the stored sender is the requester
    where the envelope reveals one, the requester is not blocked, the
    account is offline, no id has rung before, and per-(sender, addressee)
    and per-addressee limits hold. Requests may arm for 120 s. The response
    is always {} so it is not a presence oracle. Proof REQUIRED.
  - push/register 0.3: `selfControl` lets a device with no controller VTA
    register as its own controller, with an initial allowlist (normally its
    mediator), under gateway policy (push/register:selfControlRefused).
    Exactly one of controllerVtaDid / selfControl.
  - push binding 0.1 (draft, in place): §3.5 sender-requested,
    mediator-triggered wake; self-controlled handles in §3.3.

  Receipts (messaging/receipt 0.1, TSP binding 0.2):
  - messaging/receipt: a fire-and-forget Trust Task { confirms } the
    recipient's delivery layer sends to the transport-authenticated sender
    once it durably holds a message that asked for a receipt. Requested,
    never automatic; may be declined; settles only from the addressed
    party; never answered. A transition section accepts the earlier
    https://affinidi.com/delivery/1.0/receipt body alongside it.
  - TSP binding 0.2: optional `deliveryId` envelope member requests a
    receipt; envelope type unchanged, so 0.1 and 0.2 interoperate.
  - DIDComm binding 0.2 (draft, in place): §2.1, a `delivery_id` header
    requests a receipt (not `thid`, which §3.1 gives to threadId).

  Regenerates the Rust, TypeScript, Go and Dart bindings.

- **rooms**: Load-older paging by version (records/list 0.8, keys/browse 0.6) and host size limits in rooms/info 0.5 ([#1289](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1289))

rooms/records/list 0.8 adds `beforeVersion`, an exclusive upper bound on
  `version` that mirrors `sinceVersion`. Under `newestFirst` (0.7) it lets a
  reader showing a conversation from its head ask for the records before the
  oldest one it holds by naming that version, with no cursor to keep: the
  cursor is the host's, short-lived and lost with the client's state. It
  applies under either order, and a cursor now belongs to the bounds as well
  as the order it was issued under. Not `extends: "0.7"`: a 0.7 host that
  pruned the bound would answer "load older" with the room's head.

  rooms/keys/browse 0.6 passes `beforeVersion` through for a member whose
  surface reaches the room only through their key holder, and answers
  `hostRefused` rather than drop the bound against a host without
  records/list 0.8.

  rooms/info 0.5 (`extends: "0.4"`) adds two optional response members so a
  client can refuse before it writes: `maxRecordDocumentBytes`, the largest
  rooms/records/put document the host accepts (its own per-record limit,
  refused with `recordTooLarge`, never above put 0.6's declared 2 MiB), and
  `maxChunkSize`, the largest proxied chunk it admits at its own size. File
  limits and the member's allowance were already in the response (`limits`,
  `usage.member.limits`).

  Requested by a wallet integrator (OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#2294,
  points 3 and 4). `order` itself shipped in records/list 0.7 / keys/browse
  0.5 ([#1088](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1088)) and put's `maxDocumentBytes` in records/put 0.6 ([#1252](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1252)).

- **chat/direct**: A message from one person to another, rewritable by its author (chat/direct/message/0.1) ([#1066](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1066))

* feat(chat/direct): a message from one person to another, rewritable by its author (chat/direct/message/0.1)



### Build & CI

- **https**: Jsonwebtoken 11 in trust-tasks-https, jsonschema 0.60 in trust-tasks-rs ([#1290](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1290))

Aligns the two dependencies a downstream workspace (OpenVTC VTI) compiles
  twice because these crates pinned older majors: jsonschema 0.49 in
  trust-tasks-rs (`validate` feature) beside its 0.60, and jsonwebtoken 10 in
  trust-tasks-https (`jwt` feature) beside its 11.

  jsonschema is private to trust-tasks-rs (no jsonschema type is in its public
  API) and needed no code change. jsonwebtoken is public through
  `JwtBearerAuth::new(DecodingKey, Validation, _)`, so a consumer that builds
  those values with jsonwebtoken 10 must move to 11: a break of the `jwt`
  feature's API, hence the `!`. No source change was needed in this crate.



### Fixed

- **rs,https,ts,go,dart**: Refuse a document that marks an unrecognized ext namespace critical ([#1256](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1256))

* fix(rs,https,ts,go,dart)!: refuse a document that marks an unrecognized ext namespace critical

  SPEC §4.5.2 rule 4: a consumer that does not recognize a namespace named in
  extCritical MUST NOT process the document and MUST reject it with
  unsupportedExtension. No runtime read the member, so a document whose payload
  type does not model it was processed as if the namespace were absent.

  Each runtime gains a check (check_critical_extensions, checkCriticalExtensions,
  CheckCriticalExtensions) that walks the payload as received alongside its
  schema, applies rules 1, 2 and 4, and runs in every consume pipeline after
  the proof and per-specification checks and before the item-11 record. The
  recognized namespaces are a new consume-checks option, empty by default.
  Shared vectors in fixtures/consume/ext-critical.json pin the four together.

- **chat/direct**: Describe the oneOf members of message/0.1 and regenerate its bindings ([#1295](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1295))

* fix(chat/direct): describe the oneOf members of message/0.1 and regenerate its bindings

  #1066 merged with five undescribed payload members, which the description
  ratchet refuses, and with TypeScript, Go and Dart bindings generated before
  the front matter's maxDocumentBytes. Describe the members and regenerate.

body:
Four small follow-ups from the open issues.

- **PR template** (`.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md`). A short checklist: DCO sign-off, a conventional-commit title with any `!` scoped to the package, all four libraries regenerated when `specs/` changes, no version or CHANGELOG edits, and `npm run check` plus the relevant tests.

- **Developer guide.** The CI-checks table in `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md` gains the eleven `build-registry.mjs` checks it did not list: `checkPayloadSchema`, `checkProofFloor`, `checkIssuedAtFloor`, `checkFreeTextBounds`, `checkErrorCodeNamespaces`, `checkGeneratorKeywords`, `checkTargetFrameworkForm`, `checkKnownImplementationRoles`, `checkIdentifierScopeJustification`, `checkOutcomeEvidence` and `checkCommittedRecordMirror`.
