title: fix(rs,ts,ts-tsp,proof,didcomm,didcomm-v1,tsp,dart-didcomm,dart-tsp,go-didcomm,go-tsp): message bindings enforce document size bounds; shared extends routing vector
body:
## Summary

**Size bounds in the message bindings (#1121)**
- **Rust, through `GuardedConsumer`:** `consume_body` and `consume_body_dispatched` now pass the body's size as `ConsumeChecks::received_bytes`. `GuardedConsumer` is shared by the DIDComm v2.1, DIDComm v1 and TSP consumers, so a document larger than its specification's `maxDocumentBytes` is now refused `malformedRequest` in all three.
  - The refusal comes after the envelope has authenticated the sender, is addressed to that sender, and happens before the item-11 record is written.
  - Size is measured on the compact JSON text, counted without allocating, because the DIDComm stacks hand over a body that is already decoded.
  - A specification that declares no bound gets no default bound.
- **Rust core fix:** `consume_inbound` and `consume_dispatched` used to hold a document read forward along `extends` to the implemented version's bound. They no longer do, because a later version may declare a larger bound (as Go #1251 and Dart #1242 already do).
- **Dart `trust_tasks_didcomm` and `trust_tasks_tsp`:** the same rule as Rust, after `readForVersion` and before `consumeInbound`.
- **TypeScript `trust-tasks-ts-tsp`:** the same rule, before `consumeInbound`, exported as `DOCUMENT_TOO_LARGE_WIRE_MESSAGE`. It reads `SPEC.maxDocumentBytes` defensively, so it does nothing until it runs on a core release that emits the bound; published core 0.29.0 does not.

**Extends (#1117)**
- `trust-tasks-go/didcomm` and `trust-tasks-go/tsp` now require the published core **v0.11.0** and use `ReadForSpecWith`.
- Both consumers take an optional `Consumer.Extends` lookup (nil means the registry's), which is also passed to `ConsumeOptions.Extends`. A third-party (§6.5) chain is followed through it.
- New shared vector `fixtures/consume/extends-routing.json`, with 10 cases:
  - the implemented version itself, and its `#request` form;
  - a forward read one link along the chain, and one two links along, each pruned and answered typed `<received>#response`;
  - `unsupportedVersion`: a later MINOR with no declaration, a chain that does not reach the implemented version, and an earlier MINOR;
  - `unsupportedType`: another slug, the same slug under another authority, and the `#response` variant.
- It runs in all four runtimes:
  - `trust-tasks-rs/tests/extends_routing_vectors.rs`
  - `trust-tasks-ts/test/extends-routing-vectors.test.ts`
  - `trust-tasks-go/trusttasks/extends_vectors_test.go`
  - `trust-tasks-dart/test/extends_routing_vectors_test.dart`
- The vector found a TypeScript bug, fixed here: `readForSpec` refused the implemented version's own `#request` Type URI as `unsupportedType`. Its variant comparison did not treat `#request` and no fragment as the same.

**Proof (#1092)**
- `verify_raw` no longer clones the document, or the proof, to drop `proof`. It serialises a borrowed view without that member. The byte-for-byte cross-library fixtures still pass.

**Docs:** `docs/runtime-parity.md` rows for size bounds and extends, and `fixtures/consume/README.md`.

## Security notes
- No size refusal happens before transport sender authentication. Every one goes to the authenticated sender and is made before the item-11 record is written. The tests check that no id is burned and the handler does not run.
- **Known ordering difference:** Dart checks size before `consumeInbound`'s expiry, freshness and identity checks; Rust checks it after them. A document that fails both gets a different code in each runtime, but both answers go to the authenticated sender. Recorded in the parity doc.

## Still open
- **Go DIDComm and TSP:** they already pass the exact received bytes as `ConsumeOptions.Received`, but v0.11.0 predates #1251's size check. Bounds take effect when they require the next Go core release.
- **`trust-tasks-ts-tsp`:** enforcement starts once a core that emits `maxDocumentBytes` is on npm and the sibling's peer floor is raised.

## Tests
- `cargo test`: trust-tasks-rs (`--no-default-features --features acl`, plus the two new integration tests), -tsp, -didcomm, -didcomm-v1, -https, -proof (all features).
- `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -D warnings` on each touched crate, and `cargo fmt --check`.
- `dart analyze --fatal-infos` and `dart test` in trust-tasks-dart, -dart-didcomm and -dart-tsp.
- `npm test` in trust-tasks-ts and trust-tasks-ts-tsp.
- `gofmt`, `go vet` and `go test` in trust-tasks-go, /didcomm and /tsp.
- `npm run check`.

Closes #1117.
Part of #1121.
Part of #1092.

title: site: load a slim registry index and fetch each spec's detail on demand
body:
This finishes the structural part of #1145. Every visit used to download `tasks.generated.js` with every spec version's full record in it: the schema, error codes, classification rationales, parties and shared-schema uses. That held even for a deep link to a single spec. The file is now a slim registry index, and each page fetches the detail it needs when it opens.

## Measurements

These are for `tasks.generated.js` (the content-hashed copy the page loads), built from this branch's base and from this branch:

| | raw (minified) | gzip -9 (as deployed) | brotli -q 11 |
|---|---|---|---|
| before | 10,005,979 B | 1,254,312 B | 777,348 B |
| after | 939,619 B | 128,875 B | 101,813 B |

That is about 10.6 times smaller raw and about 9.7 times smaller over the wire. A deep link to a spec now also fetches one `detail.json`. Across the 1,573 detail files (1,397 versions and 176 shared schemas), the median is 5.3 KB raw, the 95th percentile is 12.2 KB and the largest is 147 KB. For example, `acl/grant/0.3` is 9.6 KB raw and 3.1 KB gzipped.

## What changed

- `scripts/build-registry.mjs`
  - `TT_TASKS` now holds only `INDEX_FIELDS`: id, slug, title, summary, category, keywords, status, version, created, updated and lifecycle. That covers what the home page, registry, categories, search, nav, page titles, version lists, related-task links and the implementations page read.
  - `TT_SHARED` drops `schema` and gains `usedByCount` and `detailPath`.
  - `TT_STATS` is computed at build time with routes.js `latestPerSlug`, because `authors` is no longer in the index. Its values match the old ones. `categories` is still counted on the page from data.js.
  - `TT_SHARED_USED_BY` is gone.
  - After the specs tree is synced, the build writes each version's full record (the same object `registry.json` carries) to `/specs/<slug>/<M.N>/detail.json`. Each shared schema gets `<name>.detail.json` beside it, holding its schema and the tasks that use it. The `.detail.json` name keeps these files out of the `*.schema.json` content-type rule in deploy.yml.
  - `registry.json` is unchanged.
- `website/assets/pages.jsx`
  - There is a small fetch cache, `fetchJson` and `useJson`, that shares in-flight requests and does not cache failures.
  - `SpecPage` looks the route up in the index as before, so not-found and deep links behave the same. `SpecLoader` then fetches the detail and renders the unchanged `SpecDetail` over the index entry merged with the detail. While it loads, or if the fetch fails, the page shows the heading, summary and lifecycle banner from the index, plus either "Loading specification…" or a failed-fetch notice with "Try again" and a GitHub link.
  - `/schema/<slug>` works the same way.
  - The schema-version diffs on both pages now fetch each side's schema, and the shared schemas it `$ref`s, only when the diff is opened. They then resolve it exactly as before. I checked this in Node: all 1,573 schemas resolve with no external `$ref` left.
- `scripts/build-website.mjs`: no change to how files are hashed. `tasks.generated.js` keeps its content-hashed, immutable copy. The detail files stay at fixed URLs under `/specs/`, which deploy.yml already serves with `max-age=300, stale-while-revalidate`. Only the comment changed.
- `.github/workflows/deploy.yml`: comments only. The detail files go up with the specs tree in step 2, before the new `index.html` in step 5, so a new index never names detail that isn't uploaded yet. The gzip-at-rest upload of the index stays.
- Tests
  - `test:website` hands the server render a fetch cache that reads the built `website/specs/`, so every spec and schema route renders in full as before.
  - Two new tests check that the index carries no detail fields, that every version and shared schema has its detail file (with the used-by count matching), and that the spec and schema pages render their heading and loading state when nothing has been fetched.
  - The per-variant proof-requirement test now finds its task through the detail files.
- `npm run smoke:website` adds `/schema/acl/_shared/0.1/acl-entry` and fails a page that is still loading after it settles or that shows a failed fetch. I checked that it catches a missing `detail.json`: it reports the 404 and the failed-fetch notice.
- `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md` describes the index and detail split and the updated checks.

## Verification

- `npm run build`
- `npm run check`: passes.
- `npm run test:website`: 50 of 50 pass.
- `npm run smoke:website`: all 6 routes pass in headless Chrome with no console errors or failed requests.
- `npm run test:infra`: 41 of 41 pass.
- `actionlint`: clean.

Closes #1145.

title: docs(examples): runnable TypeScript, Go and Dart getting-started apps with snippet drift checks
body:
GETTING-STARTED.md worked end to end only for Rust. Sections 3, 3a and 3b showed `consumeInbound` fragments with free variables (`doc`, `peerVid`, `myVerifier`, `myValidator`, `send`, `applyGrant`) and nothing checked them. This is the remaining half of #1128.

Each of the three sections is now extracted from a runnable example application, the way section 2 is extracted from `examples/getting-started`:

- `examples/getting-started-ts`: a `node:http` receiver speaking the HTTPS binding's wire format and running `consumeInbound`, a `fetch` sender, and signing and verification through `@openvtc/trust-tasks-proof`.
- `examples/getting-started-go`: the same with `net/http` and the `trust-tasks-go/proof` module. The generated package is committed, as in `consumer-app-go`.
- `examples/getting-started-dart`: `trust_tasks_https` on both ends and `trust_tasks_proof` for signing and verification.

All three pin `acl/grant/0.3` with the same `trust-tasks.toml`, lock and vendored bundle as the Rust example, and generate it with that language's generator. Each one derives the sender's `did:key` from the same seed as the Rust example. Each one runs the round trip and then asserts three more things: a byte-identical retry is absorbed and answered with the first response (item 11), a payload changed after signing is refused `proofInvalid`, and a correctly signed payload missing `purposes` is refused `malformedRequest`. Any failed assertion makes the run exit non-zero.

I wrote new examples rather than promoting the `consumer-app-*` ones because the two sets do different jobs. The consumer apps cover the generator's surface: several pinned tasks, a third-party source, extends routing, refusals, and a fixed clock. The getting-started flow is one signed task over a real transport. Merging them would make the document's snippets carry generator-coverage code, or make the consumer apps lose it. The new examples share their lock and bundle with the Rust example and reuse the consumer apps' CI jobs. The duplication left is the three vendored copies of one bundle, which every example already carries.

The validator is a deliberate stand-in. The brief allowed no third-party dependency beyond what the examples already use, and the runtimes bundle no JSON Schema engine. So each example has a small structural validator (`validator.ts`, `validator.go`, `lib/structural_validator.dart`) for the subset of JSON Schema 2020-12 the generated schemas use: local `$ref`, type, required, properties, `additionalProperties: false`, const, enum, oneOf, items and length bounds. The document says plainly that it is a stand-in and names the engine a real application would use. The Dart example declares `ssi` to build a `DidSigner`. `trust_tasks_proof` already depends on `ssi`, so the dependency graph does not change.

The drift check is `scripts/check-getting-started-snippets.mjs <example file>`. It is a plain Node script with no dependencies, so the Go and Dart jobs can run it on the runner's preinstalled Node. It uses the same markers as the Rust test: a `<!-- snippet: <file>#<region> -->` line before a fence in the document, and `// GETTING-STARTED:begin/end <region>` in the source. It fails if a snippet has drifted, if a snippet names a region that does not exist, or if a declared region is never embedded.

CI changes add steps to existing jobs and keep their names. `consumer-app-ts` in ts.yml now builds `trust-tasks-ts-proof`, then runs the example and the snippet check. `consumer-app` in go.yml generates, checks the committed tree for drift, vets and runs the example, then runs the snippet check, on both Go 1.22 and stable. `consumer-app` in dart.yml runs pub get, generate, `analyze --fatal-infos`, run and the snippet check. In dart.yml these steps are skipped on the 3.3 leg, because `trust_tasks_proof`'s floor is 3.6. The new directories are also added to dependabot and to the npm-audit matrix in advisories.yml. The audit matrix entry adds one leg to that job.

Verified locally: each example runs end to end (`npm run all`, `go generate ./... && go vet ./... && go run .`, `dart pub get` then generate, `dart analyze --fatal-infos`, `dart run bin/main.dart`). The snippet check passes for all three files. I edited one snippet line to confirm the check fails and reports the first differing line. `cargo test -p trust-tasks --test getting_started_snippets` still passes, and `npm audit --audit-level=high` in the TS example finds nothing. I have not run Go 1.22 locally; CI covers that leg.

Closes #1128.

title: spec(chat/direct/message): describe the branch constraints, and regenerate the libraries
body:
Fixes main, which has been red since #1066. That PR merged `chat/direct/message/0.1` with two problems, and every open PR now fails the same checks. The website deploy on main fails too, so trusttasks.org is not being updated.

- **The member-description ratchet (#1258).** Five schema members inside the `oneOf` branches had no `description`: the two `revision` constraints, the first revision's `body`, and the two `kind` sub-schemas that match a reaction. A new slug is allowed none. Each now has a one-line description taken from the spec's own rules: revision 1 is the first document; a rewrite is any later revision; an empty body is a withdrawal, which only a rewrite can be; a reaction must name its target in `inReplyTo`. These are text edits to five lines, with nothing else in the schema changed. The version has not been released, and a description is additive in any case.
- **Binding drift.** The committed TS, Go, Dart and Rust modules for this version did not match what the generators produce. `npm run regen` brings all four in line; only this spec's modules change.

`npm run validate`, `npm run check` and `check-bindings` pass, with all four libraries agreeing on 1,398 specifications.

Bumps [affinidi-messaging-test-mediator](https://github.com/affinidi/affinidi-messaging-mediator) from 0.16.0 to 0.50.0.
Release notes

Sourced from affinidi-messaging-test-mediator's releases.

v0.50.0

Changed — trust-tasks-rs 0.37 (breaking)

  • trust-tasks-rs / trust-tasks-proof 0.37, affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.45, affinidi-tdk 0.37, affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service 0.30. 0.37 (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf #1021) makes validate_freshness honour a stated expiresAt. Behaviour change: a consequential task that states an expiresAt is accepted until then, up to 30 days after its issuedAt, instead of being refused 5 minutes after issuedAt. A task without an expiresAt keeps the 5-minute window.

Fixed

  • The replay record now lasts as long as the document is acceptable. It was kept until issuedAt + 5 minutes + skew, or a sooner expiresAt. Under 0.37 a document with a later expiresAt stays acceptable past that, so a replay of it after the record was dropped would have executed again. retention_end is now FreshnessPolicy::record_expiry, which the 30-day horizon bounds.
  • vta-sdk still resolves trust-tasks-rs 0.36 (with affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.44 and affinidi-tdk 0.36) until the VTI moves to 0.37. No types cross between the two, and the next vta-sdk release removes the second copies.

title: test(https): order the blocking-handler test by signals, not wall-clock time
body:
`a_blocking_sync_handler_runs_on_a_multi_thread_runtime` (added in #1244) checked that a second request was answered within 250 ms while a blocking handler slept for 300 ms. A loaded CI runner can miss that with nothing wrong. It failed `cargo test (stable, full workspace)` on #1268, a docs-only PR.

The test now orders itself by signals. The slow handler records that it has entered, then blocks until the test releases it, with a 30 s cap so a broken test cannot hang the suite. The test waits for that, sends the fast request, and requires the fast request to be answered, within a 10 s bound, while the slow request is still held. Only then does it release the slow request. If the blocking handler stalled the server, the fast request could not be answered before the release, so the bound fails. The property is the same as before, without depending on timing.

`cargo test -p trust-tasks-https --test pipeline` passes (run three times), and clippy is clean.

title: build(proof, didcomm): affinidi-crypto 0.3 and the matching Affinidi releases
body:
## Summary

Moves `trust-tasks-proof` onto `affinidi-crypto` 0.3 and the Affinidi releases built on it, so its `KeyType` is the one `affinidi-data-integrity`, `affinidi-did-common` and the resolver cache SDK now use. Releasing `trust-tasks-proof` on this enables the remaining affinidi-tdk-rs release (`affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.46.4 and `affinidi-tdk` 0.44.0, affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#1117), whose publish needs a `trust-tasks-proof` on `affinidi-crypto` 0.3.

## Changes

- `trust-tasks-proof`: `affinidi-crypto` "0.3", `affinidi-data-integrity` "0.8.7", `affinidi-did-common` "0.4.7" (normal and dev), `affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk` "0.8.53"; dev `affinidi-secrets-resolver` "0.5.18" (it re-exports the 0.3 `KeyType`). No source changes: the crate reads `KeyType` only, which 0.3 did not change.
- `trust-tasks-didcomm` (dev): `affinidi-crypto` "0.3", `affinidi-messaging-didcomm` "0.15.14", `affinidi-secrets-resolver` "0.5.18". The normal `affinidi-messaging-didcomm` requirement moves to "0.15.14" as well, so the published crate cannot resolve a 0.2-based didcomm beside a 0.3-based proof stack.
- `trust-tasks-https`, `examples/getting-started` (dev / example): `affinidi-secrets-resolver` "0.5.18".
- `trust-tasks-didcomm/tests/mediator_e2e.rs` and its dev dependencies (`affinidi-messaging-test-mediator` 0.16, `affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.32, `affinidi-tdk` 0.22, `affinidi-tdk-common` 0.7) leave the tree for now. Those published versions require `affinidi-crypto` 0.2 directly and pass its key types (`PrivateKeyAgreement`, `KeyType`) into `affinidi-messaging-didcomm` / `affinidi-secrets-resolver` and the registry `trust-tasks-proof` 0.26.3, which now build on 0.3, so the dev graph no longer compiles. The test was `#[ignore]` and not run in CI. It returns with a test-mediator release on `affinidi-crypto` 0.3 (that release itself waits on this one). README and the `[patch]` comment say so.
- `Cargo.lock`: `affinidi-crypto` 0.2.11 → 0.3.1, data-integrity 0.8.7, did-common 0.4.7, cache-sdk 0.8.53, messaging-didcomm 0.15.14, messaging-didcomm-v1 0.2.4, secrets-resolver 0.5.18; the rest of the diff is the removed mediator dev graph. One `affinidi-crypto` remains in the graph.

- `trust-tasks-https/tests/pipeline.rs`: the blocking-handler timing test builds its HTTP client before the clock starts. It failed twice on this branch, and only here, at the 250 ms bound, once the dev graph changed.

Versions and changelogs are left to release-plz.

## Behaviour

**Behaviour change (R3.6).** Signing or verifying with `eddsa-rdfc-2022` (and the other RDFC suites) now requires an `@context` that defines every member of the document. `affinidi-data-integrity` 0.8.2+ expands RDFC documents in JSON-LD safe mode, so an undefined member fails with a canonicalization error instead of being left out of the signed dataset. The JCS suites (the default) are unaffected. The RDFC sign test now adds the credentials examples context (`@vocab`) beside the credentials context.

Otherwise, an application on `trust-tasks-proof` with the `affinidi` feature now resolves the `affinidi-crypto` 0.3 line of Affinidi crates (key pairs wipe their private key on drop).

title: feat(chat/direct): a message from one person to another, rewritable by its author (chat/direct/message/0.1)
body:
## What

Adds **`chat/direct/message/0.1`** (draft, category `chat`). It is a person-to-person message that its author can rewrite. It also adds the shared component **`chat/direct/_shared/0.1/direct.schema.json`**. All four libraries are regenerated.

This is the first of a short series that answers discussion #1013, "A Trust Task type for a message from one person to another". It covers the interop board's `write` scenario.

- **One task, rewritten under the same `messageId`.** The author mints a fresh 43-character `messageId`, then sends the message again with a greater `revision` to:
  - **edit** it (`editedAt` is required on every revision after the first);
  - **withdraw** it (an empty `body`, which leaves a tombstone);
  - **react** with a message of `kind: reaction`, which names its target in `inReplyTo`.
- **Error codes.**
  - `notAuthor`: a rewrite by anyone but the authenticated original author.
  - `revisionConflict`: the same revision arrives again with a different payload.
  - `rewriteInvalid`: a rewrite changes `kind`, `writtenAt`, or a reaction's `inReplyTo`.
  - Stale revisions and unknown `messageId`s are handled silently. This avoids a state oracle (SPEC §12.6).
- **Two separate dedup layers.** SPEC §7.2 item 11 still dedups by document `id`. Separately, (author, `messageId`, `revision`) absorbs a new attempt (§8.4) that carries an identical payload.
- **Schema.** `additionalProperties: false`. The revision and reaction rules are a top-level `oneOf` with two branches (first revision / rewrite). The Rust generator's existing compound-`not` pass drops that `oneOf` from the typify copy, so it is enforced at runtime, as for the other `oneOf` schemas. typify does not support `if`/`then`.
- **`payload.invalid-examples.json`** has 10 fixtures:
  - revision 1 with `editedAt`;
  - revision 1 with an empty `body`;
  - revision 2 without `editedAt`;
  - a reaction without `inReplyTo`;
  - a `messageId` of the wrong length;
  - an unknown member;
  - an extra member in `inReplyTo`;
  - a non-`Z` `writtenAt`;
  - `revision: 0`;
  - a bare `ext` key.
- **`website/assets/data.js`**: only the `chat` category blurb changes, so that it names both `chat/direct/*` and `chat/message`. No taxonomy change is needed: `chat` is already in the meta-schema enum and in `TT_CATEGORIES`. The slug is not reserved, and the existing Rust `chat` feature covers it.

## Why this shape

- **Its own namespace, not an extension of `chat/message/0.1`.** That spec is the bridge's agent-to-platform chain. Its authority, its proof requirement (`REQUIRED`), its parties and its retention (`durable`) all differ, so an `extends` could not keep its promises.
- **Groups stay in `rooms/*`.** With pairwise identifiers, a group built by fanning out 1:1 messages cannot name its members to each other.

## Proof and carriage

`proofRequirement: OPTIONAL`, with a normative carriage rule:

- A producer **MUST** send these documents only over a binding mode whose binding specification permits omitting `proof` under SPEC §9.1.1.
- It **SHOULD NOT** fall back to a mode without that allowance; it waits or tells its user instead.
- A present proof is still verified (§7.2 item 7).

The spec names no bindings. Which modes qualify is left to each binding's own text.

## Alignment with rooms

The content vocabulary is the one in `rooms/_shared/0.1` (`SealedRecordBody`). `kind`, `writtenAt` and `editedAt` are **`$ref`'d directly** from `rooms/_shared/0.1/room.schema.json` (`RecordKind`, `RecordWrittenAt`, `RecordEditedAt`), so their patterns cannot drift. The bundle's `defOrigins` names the rooms component. The spec applies the named rooms rules (*Edits*, *What a new version keeps*, *Withdrawing a message*, *Replies*, *Reactions*, *Counting reactions*, *A reaction's value*, *Nothing answers a reaction*, *When it was written*), with host times mapped to the consumer's receipt instants.

| `chat/direct/message` | rooms | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `kind` (required) | `RecordKind` (optional) | `$ref`; stricter |
| `body` (≤16384; empty = withdrawn on a rewrite) | `body` | same rules; stricter bound |
| `writtenAt` / `editedAt` | `RecordWrittenAt` / `RecordEditedAt` | `$ref`; `editedAt` required on revision ≥ 2 |
| `inReplyTo` → `{messageId}` | `RecordReference {key, version?}` | same rules; no host version |
| edit / withdraw / react = rewrite of the same id | same | aligned; the word "retract" is kept out (it is a curator act in rooms) |
| `messageId` (author-minted) | record `key` | kept: there is no host location |
| `revision` (author-set) | `version` (host-set) | kept: there is no host |
| author = authenticated issuer; non-author rewrite refused | signed `author`; non-author rewrite shown as the new author | kept (stricter) |
| `ext` | — | kept; dropped on import |
| no `title`/`tags`/provenance/`roomProfile` | present | omitted; a direct message is a strict subset |

The cost of the `$ref` is that `chat/direct` follows the lifecycle of `rooms/_shared`. `rooms/_shared/0.1` and `0.2` define these four definitions byte-identically. A container-neutral content component that both families reference would be the longer-term option, and that is for the rooms owner.

## Not in this PR (follow-ups)

- **Binding text.** Each binding would say what its sender authentication gives a holder of the envelope. That is deferred.
- **`chat/direct/receipt/0.1`.** Delivered/read receipts, opt-in by the reader. When it lands, `related` here gains it.
- **`knownImplementations`** for both tasks, after the first interop run.
- **`chat/direct/message/0.2`.** An optional `file` aligned with the rooms `FileManifest`, `extends: "0.1"`.
- **Canonical framework repo** (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec), not here:
  - **C1:** a way for a specification to say its documents are meant to be non-transferable, so that "SHOULD NOT include a proof" can be said without weakening §4.7.2.
  - **C2:** an informative §13 item on this kind of carriage.
  - **C3:** only if pursued, an in-band authentication construction that does not conflict with §4.7.3 item 1.
- **For the rooms owner:** an import provision, so that history imported from a 1:1 is not flagged as backdated.

## Other notes for review

- **`targetFrameworkVersion` is `0.6.0`.** The build has no `specs/_framework/0.7` envelope schema yet, and the scaffolder chose 0.6.0.
- **The acceptance window (30 days) is guidance.** It is stated as a SHOULD in Security & Privacy, for offline composition and mediated delivery.
- **No version bumps, CHANGELOG entries or `SPEC.md` edits.** `rooms/*` and `chat/message` are untouched.

## Testing

All commands were run locally under `nice -n 10`.

- `npm run validate`: passes. `TT_STRICT_SECURITY_PRIVACY=1 npm run validate` also passes. Casing, wire conventions, stale references and the free-text bound all report 0 non-conforming.
- `npm run build`: passes. The six request examples and two error examples validate against the envelope schema.
- Libraries regenerated with `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all`, `npm run build-ts-bindings`, `npm run build-go-bindings` and `npm run build-dart-bindings`. All four succeed; the drift is committed.
- `npm run check-bindings`: all four libraries agree across 1341 specs.
- `npm run check-published-schemas`: passes (new versions only).
- `npm run check-withdrawal-readiness`: passes.
- `npm run build-bundles && npm run check-bundles`: 1335 bundles verified. The new bundle's `defOrigins` names `rooms/_shared/0.1`.
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --no-default-features --features chat`: passes. With `--features "chat validate" --test conformance chat::direct`, all 7 tests pass: the 6 examples and `rejects_invalid_examples`.
- `cargo clippy -p trust-tasks-rs --lib --test conformance --no-default-features --features "chat validate" -- -D warnings`: clean.
- `trust-tasks-ts`:
  - `npx tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit` passes;
  - `npm test` passes (126/126);
  - `npm run smoke` passes.
- `trust-tasks-go`:
  - `go build ./...` passes;
  - `go vet` on `./specs/chat/...` and `./trusttasks/...` passes;
  - `go test` on `./trusttasks/...`, `./smoke/...` and `./specs/chat/...` passes;
  - `gofmt -l specs/chat` reports nothing.
- `trust-tasks-dart`: `dart analyze --fatal-infos lib/specs/chat test` finds no issues. `dart test test/smoke_test.dart` passes.
- Not run locally:
  - the full `cargo build --workspace --all-targets`;
  - workspace-wide clippy;
  - the API-compatibility jobs.

  CI covers them.

title: fix(rs,https,ts,go,dart)!: refuse a document that marks an unrecognized ext namespace critical
body:
SPEC §4.5.2 rule 4: "A *consumer* that does not recognize a critical namespace **MUST NOT** process the document, and **MUST** reject it with `unsupportedExtension`." §7.2 says the same about `ext`. Rule 2 adds that an entry naming a namespace absent from the sibling `ext` is rejected with `malformedRequest`.

None of the four runtimes read `extCritical`. All four define the `unsupportedExtension` code, but no pipeline ever produced it. Two things followed:

- When a payload type does not model the member, the typed decode drops it. Under `acceptUnvalidated`, the default for the message bindings when no validator is configured, the handler then ran as if the namespace were absent. This is the outcome the marking exists to prevent.
- When a specification does model it (`vtc/join-requests/manifest`, `vtc/_shared/schema-registry`), nothing compared the listed namespaces with what the consumer implements.

## What changed

**A check, in all four runtimes.** It is `check_critical_extensions` (Rust), `checkCriticalExtensions` (TS, Dart) and `CheckCriticalExtensions` (Go). It reads a payload against the payload schema of the specification it is consumed under:

- **Where it looks.** The member exists only at the object levels a specification opts in at, so the payload is walked alongside its schema. It follows local `$ref`s and every `allOf` / `anyOf` / `oneOf` branch, `properties`, `additionalProperties`, `patternProperties` (taken whole), `items` and `prefixItems`.
  - A level whose schema declares `extCritical` is checked.
  - A level the schema closes (`additionalProperties: false` / `unevaluatedProperties: false`) without declaring it is refused `malformedRequest` when the member is present. A validator would report the same thing; this applies it under `acceptUnvalidated` too, so the marking is never dropped silently.
  - An open level is data and is not read. Examples are the document a `vault/sign-trust-task` caller asks to have signed, and an `ext` namespace's own content.
  - With no schema (a hand-written `SpecPolicy` without `payloadSchema`), every level outside `ext` content is read.
- **What it checks there.**
  - Rules 1 and 2 → `malformedRequest`: the member must be a non-empty array of unique strings, each matching the reverse-DNS grammar and each naming an immediate key of the sibling `ext`.
  - Rule 4 → `unsupportedExtension` (not retryable) for the first namespace the consumer does not recognize. The message names that namespace, cut to 128 characters.
- **Cost.**
  - A payload with no member named `extCritical` costs one linear scan, and the schema is not read.
  - Otherwise the walk has a step budget (100,000 plus 64 per value) and a depth limit of 128. Past either, the document is refused `malformedRequest` rather than passed.

**Where it runs.** It runs in `consume_inbound` / `consume_dispatched` / `consume_dispatched_answer` (Rust, via `consume_core`) and `consumeInbound` / `ConsumeInbound` (TS, Go, Dart). Since #1244 the Rust `HttpsServer` runs `consume_dispatched_answer`, so it gets the check from there and runs it once. The Rust/Go/Dart message bindings and the Dart HTTPS server also reach it through these.

- **Order.** After the proof and per-specification checks, so an unauthenticated sender learns nothing about which namespaces a consumer implements. Before the item-11 record, so a refused document never burns its `id`.
- **Which payload is read.** The payload is read from the document **as received** where the pipeline has it (`VerifyReceived` / `with_received` in Rust, `Received` in Go, `received` in Dart, the received object in TS), because a typed decode drops the member. On a forward reading along `extends`, the unpruned received payload is read against the implemented version's schema.

**Recognized namespaces** are a new consume-checks option, empty by default:

- Rust: `ConsumeChecks::with_recognized_extensions` (`recognized_extensions` field), `GuardedConsumer::with_recognized_extensions`, `HttpsServerBuilder::recognized_extensions`.
- TS: `ConsumeChecks.recognizedExtensions`.
- Go: `ConsumeChecks.RecognizedExtensions`.
- Dart: `ConsumeChecks(recognizedExtensions:)` / `withRecognizedExtensions`.

The Rust HTTPS server passes `HttpsServerBuilder::recognized_extensions` into its `ConsumeChecks` (`with_recognized_extensions`). The schema for the walk comes from the dispatcher registration (`AsyncDispatcher` already records each `P::PAYLOAD_SCHEMA`), so the server keeps no schema of its own.

## Behaviour changes (R3.6)

- A document that marks a namespace critical is now refused `unsupportedExtension` unless the consumer lists that namespace. Before, it was processed.
- A malformed `extCritical` (rules 1 and 2), or one at a level whose schema does not allow it, is now refused `malformedRequest` even under `acceptUnvalidated`.
- No conforming document without `extCritical` is affected. A payload member literally named `extCritical` inside an open object is not read.
- Rust API breaks:
  - `RejectReason` gains `UnsupportedExtension { namespace }`. The enum is not `#[non_exhaustive]`.
  - `ConsumeChecks` gains a public field, so struct literals need `recognized_extensions: &[]`.
- TS, Go and Dart: additive API (an optional option), with the behaviour break above. Hence `!` on all five scopes, as in #1162.

## Not done here

- **Sibling packages are not wired yet.** These are the TS `trust-tasks-ts-tsp`, the Go `didcomm` / `tsp` modules, and the Dart `trust_tasks_https` / `trust_tasks_didcomm` / `trust_tasks_tsp`. They build against the published core, so they cannot name the new option until that core is released. They get the check now and recognize no namespace. The gap is recorded in `docs/runtime-parity.md`.
- **The Rust binding wrappers.** `DidcommConsumer`, `TspConsumer` and `DidcommV1Consumer` construct their `GuardedConsumer` internally. Exposing the option on them is a follow-up.
- **Response documents.** Clients reading a `#response` (for example, an applicant reading a `vtc/join-requests/manifest` response) do not run this check. `check_critical_extensions` and its ports are public for that caller.

## Tests

- **Shared vectors.** `fixtures/consume/ext-critical.json` has 18 cases against `fixtures/consume/ext-critical.schema.json`, run by `trust-tasks-rs/tests/ext_critical.rs`, `trust-tasks-ts/test/ext-critical.test.ts`, `trust-tasks-go/trusttasks/ext_critical_test.go` and `trust-tasks-dart/test/ext_critical_test.dart`.
- **Pipeline test.** Each of those files also drives the pipeline. A document whose payload type models only `subject` is refused `unsupportedExtension` without running the handler, and is then handled by a consumer that recognizes the namespace, which shows that no record was written.
- **Rust.** `trust-tasks-rs/src/critical.rs` has unit tests for the namespace grammar and the depth limit. `trust-tasks-https/tests/end_to_end.rs` adds `a_critical_namespace_is_understood_or_refused` (422 `unsupportedExtension`, then 200).

Only `cargo fmt`, `gofmt` and `dart format` were run locally. CI runs the tests.

## Checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): n/a (a test uses `reqwest::Client::new()` as the existing tests do)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1): the refusal runs before the item-11 claim, so nothing is recorded for a refused document
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4): n/a; `unsupportedExtension` is not retryable
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*): no wire type changes; the newly emitted `unsupportedExtension` is in `trust-task-error/0.6`, which all four already emit; all four runtimes are changed together (R3.6 above)
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*): no recognized namespaces by default; a walk over its budget or depth refuses
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*): n/a
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): no mutations
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers: none

title: fix(infra): verify.sh sends an Origin, so its CORS check tests what a browser sees
body:
The response headers policy (`response-headers-policy.json`) is now applied to the trusttasks.org distribution. `./verify.sh` then failed one check: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` absent on `/spec/acl/grant/0.1`.

The distribution was right and the check was wrong. CloudFront adds a response headers policy's CORS headers only when the request carries an `Origin` header, as a browser's cross-origin `fetch` does, and `verify.sh`'s curl sent none. With `Origin` set, the live response carries `access-control-allow-origin: *` alongside `vary: Accept, Accept-Encoding`.

`check_header` now sends `Origin: https://example.org` on every header check, and a comment says why. Against the live site, every check passes: negotiation, the JSON 404s, and all security, CORS and `Vary` headers.

title: site: fix the axe accessibility findings (ARIA on card keywords, contrast, focusable code blocks, headings, landmarks)
body:
An axe-core 4.10.2 scan of trusttasks.org found six rules violated. This fixes each one in the page code (`website/assets/components.jsx`, `pages.jsx`, `site.css`, `style.css`).

The registry cards' keywords were spans carrying `aria-pressed` inside the card's link, which made them toggles that a keyboard could never reach (a link can't contain a control). They are plain tags now. The active keyword is still highlighted, and the filter rail's real buttons remain the toggles. The mouse-only "click a keyword on a card to filter" shortcut is gone: a click on a card now opens the spec.

The chip counts (`.tt-chip__count`) dimmed the muted text colour to 0.7 opacity, giving 3.6:1 at about 10px. They now inherit the chip's own colour, which is 4.5:1 or better on every chip background in both themes, the pressed navy chip included.

`CodeBlock`'s `<pre>` is now a focusable group with a name ("JSON code", "Rust code", and so on). Rendered prose goes through a new `TTProse` component, which does the same for any `<pre>` that actually scrolls and re-checks on resize, so short examples don't each become a tab stop. Both get a visible `:focus-visible` outline in `--tt-link`. The ceremony page's definition `<pre>` gets the same treatment. I used `role="group"` rather than `region` so that a page of code blocks doesn't turn into a page of landmarks.

Headings: the home page's framework-specification card, the category tiles and the About page's cards each sat two levels below the heading before them. They now use the next level down, styled at their old size.

The "On this page" asides on spec, binding and shared-schema pages were complementary landmarks nested inside `<main>`. They are now `<nav aria-label="On this page">`.

The "nothing registered" pages for a spec, binding, ceremony and shared schema (for example `/spec/nope/0.1`) had no h1. Each now has one, styled as the bold line it replaces, so the route-change focus move from #1217 lands on it. The generic `NotFoundPage` already had an h1.

While re-checking other routes I also fixed one minor issue: an empty `<th>` in rendered prose (a row-label column in `/specification`) is replaced with an empty `<td>` (axe `empty-table-header`).

Before, against a local build of `main`: 7 rules and 309 nodes. That was aria-allowed-attr 279 (critical), color-contrast 22, scrollable-region-focusable 2, heading-order 2, landmark-complementary-is-top-level 2, page-has-heading-one 1 and empty-table-header 1, spread over `/`, `/registry`, `/spec/acl/grant/0.3`, `/binding/https/0.3`, `/spec/nope/0.1`, `/categories` and `/specification`. The scan was at 1280px in the default light theme. Dark mode was checked by reading the token values, not by scanning.

title: feat(go): ConsumeReceived, the inbound body the message bindings share, and NewURNUUID
body:
The `trust-tasks-go/tsp` and `trust-tasks-go/didcomm` consumers each carry their own copy of the inbound body: the `refused` closure, the raw parse, the case-fold check, `ReadForSpecWith`, the decode, `documentWith`, `asReceived`, the policy wiring and the reply switch. The copies have already drifted. On a body that does not parse, TSP addresses the error from the routing members that did parse, and DIDComm addresses it from an empty document. The two also send different messages. This PR adds that body to the core, once, so each binding can keep only the code that opens its envelope and its own checks.

## The API (additive)

```go
func ConsumeReceived[P, R any](ctx, received json.RawMessage, transport TransportHandler,
    spec SpecPolicy, decode func(json.RawMessage) (P, error), handler Handler[P, R],
    opts ReceiveOptions) (ReceivedOutcome[R], error)

type ReceiveOptions struct {
    ProofPolicy; PayloadPolicy; Checks ConsumeChecks   // ConsumeOptions' own; required as there
    Extends ExtendsLookup; MyVID string; Now time.Time; NewErrorID func() string; Clock Clock
    BindingCheck func(*Document[json.RawMessage]) *RejectReason   // e.g. DIDComm §3.1
}
type ReceivedOutcome[R any] struct { Outcome ConsumeOutcome[R]; Reply json.RawMessage }

func NewURNUUID() string                // v4 urn:uuid, panics if crypto/rand fails
var ErrNoAuthenticatedSender error
const MalformedDocumentWireMessage, CaseFoldedMembersWireMessage, PayloadMismatchWireMessage
```

The steps run in the same order the bindings use today:

1. A body that does not parse gets `malformedRequest`, addressed from whichever routing members did parse. This is the TSP behaviour, and it becomes the shared one.
2. `BindingCheck`, if the binding set one.
3. Members whose names differ only by case, anywhere in the document, get `malformedRequest`.
4. `ReadForSpecWith(received, spec, opts.Extends)` reads a later version forward along its extends chain, so a nil lookup falls back to the registry index. A document of another specification is refused `unsupportedType`, and an older version the chain does not reach is refused `unsupportedVersion`.
5. `decode`. A decode failure gets `malformedRequest`.
6. `ConsumeInbound` runs with `Received: received`. The proof is verified over the received bytes, the item-11 digest is taken over the received bytes, and `maxDocumentBytes` (#1251) is enforced for a document of the spec's own version.

Every refusal happens before the replay record is written. Replies go back to the sender the transport authenticated. `ConsumeReceived` refuses a transport with no authenticated sender (`ErrNoAuthenticatedSender`), because its early answers are only safe when they go to the authenticated party. A transport with no authenticated sender should use `ConsumeInbound`.

Some choices worth checking in review:

- The policies are `ConsumeOptions`' own and still required. An unset `PayloadPolicy` or `Checks` returns `ErrMissingOption`. This check now runs before any document is read, so a misconfigured consumer fails on its first message, not on the first message that parses. The bindings keep their `Consumer` fields and map them onto these options.
- `MyVID` defaults to the transport's `DeriveParties().Recipient`. That is what both bindings pass today (`transport.Local`).
- The bindings' `asReceived` wrapper is not carried over. Once `Received` is set, the core already verifies the proof over those bytes.

## Not in this PR

The nested modules are unchanged, because they must require a core that is already published. A follow-up moves `tsp` and `didcomm` onto `ConsumeReceived`, and `tsp`, `didcomm` and `capabilityclient` onto `NewURNUUID`, once the core release that contains this change is on proxy.golang.org. After that move, each binding is just: unpack the envelope, set the binding-specific `BindingCheck` (the §3.1 thread cross-check, for DIDComm), and make one call.

## Tests

`trusttasks/receive_test.go` covers:

- a handled document and its reply, plus a duplicate answered with the retained response
- fire-and-forget, which sends no reply
- each early refusal: an unparsable member, a non-object body, a case-folded duplicate, a decode failure, `BindingCheck`, `unsupportedType`, `unsupportedVersion` and an oversized document. For each one the test asserts the code, the wire message, that the consumer is the issuer, that the handler did not run and that nothing was claimed in the record
- routing members read from an unparsable body
- an oversized document refused without using up its id
- the received-bytes digest, where a difference in an unmodelled member is an `idConflict`
- proof verification over the received bytes
- forward reading along extends, with the pruned payload and the reply typed `0.3#response`
- `identityMismatch` answered to the authenticated sender
- misconfiguration errors
- the format and uniqueness of `NewURNUUID`

How it was checked: gofmt, `go vet ./...` and `go test ./...` in `trust-tasks-go` on Go 1.27.4. `npm run regen` left no drift, and `npm run check` passes (it includes `check-release-lists`).

Part of #1110.

title: feat(go): generate the extends index into the core, so the runtime no longer imports the prebuilt tree
body:
This is step 1 of 3 toward #1112, moving the generated prebuilt tree (`trust-tasks-go/specs`, 34 MB) out of the core module. It is additive.

## What changes

- `scripts/build-go-bindings.mjs` now writes the registry's declared-extension index into the runtime's own package, as `trust-tasks-go/trusttasks/extends_index.go` (`registryExtendsIndex`). This is the only generated file outside `specs/`. Each run overwrites it, `clean()` never deletes it, and the in-process gofmt covers it. The generator is still independent of the TS and Dart generators.
- `trusttasks.RegistryExtends` reads that index, and so do `ReadForSpec`, `ExtendsChainReaches` and `ConsumeInbound`'s type check, which go through it. Behaviour is unchanged: a fragment is ignored, only the direct declaration is returned, and the entries are the same.
- **The core no longer imports `…/trust-tasks-go/specs`.** `go list -deps ./trusttasks | grep specs` is now empty.
- `specs.ExtendsOf` is still generated, so code that imports package `specs` still compiles. It is now marked `// Deprecated: use trusttasks.RegistryExtends` and forwards to it. This direction has no import cycle: `specs` imports the runtime, not the other way round.
- The `bindings-drift` job in `go.yml` now also covers `trust-tasks-go/trusttasks/extends_index.go`.
- `cmd/trust-tasks-gen`'s equivalence test now compares the consumer-side index against `trusttasks/extends_index.go`. It also fixes a quiet weakness: the entry regex allowed only one space after the colon. gofmt aligns the values, so the test was reading and comparing just 3 of the 33 entries. It now reads all 33, and they are equal.
- The `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md` extends paragraph names the new file.

Users of `cmd/trust-tasks-gen` are unaffected. Their generated `ExtendsOf` still falls back to `trusttasks.RegistryExtends`, which now carries the registry chain without the prebuilt tree.

## The sequence for #1112

The split can't be done in one PR. Any `trust-tasks-go/specs` module that requires a published core (v0.11.1 or earlier) fails with `ambiguous import: found package …/specs/… in multiple modules`, because those cores still contain the tree. The specs module's first `go.mod` therefore has to name a core release that has already dropped `specs/`. We don't use a `replace` directive or a pseudo-version.

1. **This PR (`feat(go)`, additive).** The runtime stops importing the tree. Release the core.
2. **`feat(go)!: move the generated specification packages into their own module`.** Add `trust-tasks-go/specs/go.mod`. The next core release then ships without the tree. The specs module stays unreleased and is not built in CI. It needs a "not released yet" allowance in `check-release-lists`, like `tsp` has, plus entries in both core `:(exclude)` lists. Release the core. Users of prebuilt packages stay on core v0.11.x until step 3; v0.11.x is self-contained, so it keeps working.
3. **Point `specs/go.mod` at that core and wire up its release.** That means the `go.yml` job, the `GO_MODULES` entry, a `publish-go` matrix leg with tag prefix `trust-tasks-go/specs/vX.Y.Z`, a `release-bump-go.sh` arm, and updates to the smoke test, examples, `docs/packages/go.md` and `RELEASING.md`. Then release `trust-tasks-go/specs`.

## How it was checked

- gofmt, plus `go vet ./...` and `go test ./...` in `trust-tasks-go`
- `go vet` in both Go examples
- the equivalence test, run against freshly built bundles (`TRUST_TASKS_BUNDLES=…`): 1399 packages, extends index 33 entries, equal
- `node --test scripts/test-checks/go-bindings-names.test.mjs`
- `npm run regen`, which leaves no drift
- `npm run check`, which passes and includes `check-bindings` and `check-release-lists`

Part of #1112.

title: site: group the registry's spec families
body: The registry list showed one card per slug — 344 for the Governance category alone. It now collapses each **slug family** into one row that names the family and its count (`git-ns/account/* 4 specifications`), with its categories and the first few titles as a preview. ## Which slugs group - A slug's family is its **first two segments** when it has three or more (`governance/capability/grant` → `governance/capability`), and its **first segment** when it has two (`acl/grant` → `acl`). A one-segment slug (`trust-task-ok`) has none. A slug that is itself another slug's family (`witness/session` beside `witness/session/open`) joins that family. - A family groups when **at least 3** of the *listed* specifications (latest version per slug, after filters) belong to it. Smaller families stay as flat cards. Grouping is worked out on the filtered list, so a search with two hits in a family shows two cards, not a group of two. - On today's registry that gives 106 families covering 819 of 901 slugs. `/registry/governance` goes from 344 cards to 35 groups plus the ungrouped cards. The logic is `slugFamily` / `groupFamilies` in `website/assets/routes.js` (a plain script), so Node tests it directly. ## Behaviour - With no search, keyword or status filter (including a category-only view), every family **starts closed**. Under one of those filters every family still listed holds a match, so they **start open**. A click flips one family until the filters change, and the toggles are kept per filter set, so a new filter shows the default on its first render. - Filters stay in the URL (#1217): nothing new goes into it, and Back/Forward and shared links behave as before. "Show more" now pages through rows, where a group counts as one row. The results bar adds "N families grouped". ## Accessibility - The toggle is a `

> 1. Merge, and let `deploy.yml` upload `pages/`.
> 2. From the repo root, run `npm run build:cloudfront`. It writes `infra/cloudfront/build/type-uri-negotiation.min.js` (4,050 of 10,240 bytes).
> 3. `aws cloudfront update-function … --function-code fileb://build/type-uri-negotiation.min.js`, then `test-function` on DEVELOPMENT, then `publish-function` (the README's "Update the published function" commands; carry the `Comment` forward).
> 4. Run `infra/cloudfront/verify.sh`. Its new "Static pages for crawlers" checks fail until step 3 is done.

## Problem (#1151)

The site is a single-page app. A client that runs no script, such as a search crawler or the link preview in Slack, iMessage or LinkedIn, saw the shell's site-wide title and "Loading the registry…" for every specification. `app.jsx` already sets the title, description, canonical link and `og:`/`twitter:` tags per route, but only once the page runs.

## What this does

**Build.** `scripts/build-website.mjs` (run by `npm run build`, in the same step that writes `index.html`) now writes one copy of the built `index.html` for each of:

| Route | File |
|---|---|
| `/spec/<slug>/<M.N>`, every version the registry lists (1,405) | `website/pages/spec/<slug>/<M.N>/index.html` |
| `/binding/<slug>/<M.N>` (10) | `website/pages/binding/…/index.html` |
| `/schema/<slug…>`, every shared schema (177) | `website/pages/schema/…/index.html` |
| `/ceremony/<slug>/<M.N>` (1) | `website/pages/ceremony/…/index.html` |

Each copy has that route's `<title>`, meta description, canonical link, `og:url`/`og:title`/`og:description` and the `twitter:` pair filled in. It also has the page's heading, summary and key facts as escaped HTML where `<!--tt-static-->` sits inside the boot message: breadcrumbs, Type/Binding/Schema/Definition URI, version, status, lifecycle with a link to the successor, category, keywords, dates, and links to the Markdown and the schema. The scripts are byte-for-byte `index.html`'s, so in a browser the app renders over it exactly as it does over the shell. The data comes from the scripts the page already loads (`tasks.generated.js`, `bindings.js`, `ceremonies.js`, `data.js`), so the slim index and detail-on-demand design (#1270/#1145) is untouched. No `detail.json` is read. `pages/` is emptied on every build, so a page whose route has gone does not linger.

`routeMeta` in `app.jsx` now also gives a shared schema its description, so the client agrees with the static copy.

**CloudFront function.** There is a new section 4 in `type-uri-negotiation.js`. It runs after Type URI and ceremony negotiation and after the JSON-only 404. When the `User-Agent` matches `CRAWLER_UA`, it rewrites those four route shapes to `/pages/<route>/index.html`. Segments are checked against a grammar that refuses `.`/`..`, a versioned route needs `M.N`, and a trailing slash is tolerated. `CRAWLER_UA` covers search crawlers and the preview fetchers of Slack, X, Facebook/iMessage, LinkedIn, Discord, Telegram, WhatsApp, Mastodon and Bluesky.

**Why crawlers only, and not every HTML request:** the function cannot see whether a copy exists. A route the registry does not hold has none, so S3 answers 404. For a crawler that is right: an honest 404 rather than a soft 404 under a 200. For a person it would replace the SPA's not-found page, which lists the versions that do exist, with S3's XML error. It would also break `verify.sh`'s existing guarantee that `/spec/does-not-exist/0.1` as `text/html` is a 200. So browsers keep the shell. Either way they get the same page, since both files load the same app. If the distribution later gets a 404 custom error response that serves `/index.html` **with status 404**, the user-agent test can go and every HTML request can get its copy. The README says so.

Unchanged: Type URI negotiation for JSON `Accept` (a crawler asking for `application/schema+json` still gets the schema, which is tested), the SPA fallback for everything else, and `ROOT_FILES`/`ASSET_PREFIXES`. `/pages/` is deliberately not an asset prefix, so a copy is reachable only through the rewrite.

**Deploy.** `pages/` goes up in `deploy.yml`'s step 5 sync, the one that uploads `index.html`. That gives it the same `no-cache` header, the same position after the content-hashed scripts it names, and the same `--delete` when a route leaves the registry. The step's comment explains why it must not get a slice of its own with a longer max-age: a cached copy would name scripts that step 6 has since removed.

## Size and build time

- **1,593 pages, 10.0 MB on disk** (about 6.3 KB each raw, about 2.3 KB each gzipped; CloudFront compresses `text/html`). Writing them takes **about 0.4–0.9 s** of the build (logged by the build). The full `npm run build` measured 4.9 s on origin/main and 10.8–13.8 s on this branch, but on a loaded machine. The static-page step itself is under a second.
- Every deploy re-uploads all of `pages/`, as it already does for the specs tree and the `detail.json`s, because `aws s3 sync` compares mtimes and the build rewrites them. `--size-only` is not safe here: a new bundle hash leaves the size unchanged.
- Function: 3,068 → **4,050 bytes** minified, of the 10,240-byte cap.

## Tests

- `type-uri-negotiation.test.mjs` (run against the source and the minified build) checks that:
  - each route kind maps to its copy, and a trailing slash still maps;
  - 11 real crawler and unfurler user agents match, with any `Accept`;
  - Chrome keeps the shell, for known routes and for unknown ones;
  - a crawler still gets negotiated schemas and definitions, and still gets the JSON 404;
  - routes with no copy stay with the SPA;
  - traversal and out-of-grammar segments are refused;
  - the asset trees are left alone.
- `website-jsx.test.mjs` checks that:
  - `website/pages/` holds exactly one page per spec version, binding, shared schema and ceremony;
  - each page's title, `og:title`, description, canonical link and `og:url` equal what `app.jsx`'s `routeMeta()` gives for that route;
  - each page has a static `<h1>` and is otherwise identical to `index.html`;
  - text is escaped.
- `serve-website.mjs` now passes `User-Agent` to the function, so the local preview routes crawlers as production does (`curl -A Googlebot/2.1 …`).
- `smoke:website` also loads a spec, a binding and a shared schema **as Googlebot**. Each must be served its static page (own `<title>`, static summary, canonical link in the HTML as sent), and the app must then render over it with no console error, CSP violation or failed request. The page-ready wait now also waits for the boot message to be gone, because a static page has an `<h1>` before the app runs.
- `verify.sh` gains a "Static pages for crawlers" block. Googlebot and Slackbot get the copies for each route kind, a browser still gets the site title, and `/spec/does-not-exist/0.1` is 404 for a crawler and 200 for a browser. I ran it against the local `serve-website.mjs`: everything passes except HSTS, which cannot be sent over plain HTTP.

Run locally: `npm run build`, `npm run check`, `npm run test:website` (51 pass), `npm run smoke:website` (9 runs), `npm run test:infra` (51 + 40 pass), `actionlint`.

Closes #1151.

pull request by that language's API compatibility check (`rs`, `ts`, `go` and

body:
site: static per-spec pages for crawlers and link previews (#1308)

The build writes a copy of index.html for every specification version,
binding, shared schema and ceremony under website/pages/<route>/index.html,
with that route's title, description, canonical link and og:/twitter: tags
(the same values app.jsx's routeMeta sets) and an escaped HTML summary in
the boot message; the scripts are unchanged, so the app renders over it.

The CloudFront function serves the copy to crawlers and link unfurlers
(CRAWLER_UA) for those routes, after Type URI negotiation. Browsers keep the
shell: the function cannot see whether a copy exists, and an unknown route
must keep the SPA's not-found page for a person, while a crawler gets an
honest 404. deploy.yml uploads pages/ in index.html's no-cache sync.

title: site: group the registry's spec families (#1306)
body:
site: group the registry's spec families (#1306)

The registry list collapses each slug family -- three or more of the listed
specifications sharing a family prefix (the first two segments of a deeper
slug, the first segment of a two-segment one) -- into one collapsible row
naming the family and its count. Families start closed without a search,
keyword or status filter, and open under one, since every family left in
the list then holds a match. The toggle is a button with aria-expanded and
aria-controls inside an h3; cards inside a family are h4, under a new
visually hidden h2.

title: fix(go-didcomm,go-tsp): require core v0.11.1 so the message bindings enforce document size bounds
body:
The Go DIDComm and TSP nested modules already pass the exact received document bytes to ConsumeInbound (#1263). They required core v0.11.0, though, and that release came before the per-type maxDocumentBytes check (#1251), so the bound was never applied there. Core v0.11.1 is on proxy.golang.org and has the check. This PR moves both modules to it. The proof and capabilityclient modules move from v0.10.26 to v0.11.1 as well. examples/getting-started-go's go.mod picks the new version up through go mod tidy. Its replace directive still points at the in-tree core, so nothing it builds against changes.

New tests: size_bound_test.go in trust-tasks-go/didcomm and in trust-tasks-go/tsp, following the Rust and Dart tests from #1263. A document from an authenticated sender that is over its type's bound gets a malformedRequest reply carrying DocumentTooLargeWireMessage, addressed to that sender. The handler does not run and the replay record stays empty. The same id within the bound is then handled normally. The existing received-digest tests in both modules no longer skip, because the linked core now digests Received.

docs/runtime-parity.md: the size-bound row now says the Go DIDComm and TSP consumers enforce the bound, and drops them from the open items. The extends row now names core v0.11.1.

How it was checked: gofmt, go vet ./... and go test ./... in didcomm, tsp, proof and capabilityclient on Go 1.27.4. didcomm, proof and capabilityclient were also run on Go 1.22.12. For both examples, go generate leaves the committed tree unchanged, and go vet and go run pass on 1.27.4. On 1.22.12, go vet passes for both examples, but go run aborts in dyld on this macOS ('missing LC_UUID'). That is an old-toolchain linker problem with the current macOS, not a problem in the code; CI's ubuntu 1.22 leg covers it.

Closes #1121.

The DIDComm and TSP nested modules already hand ConsumeInbound the exact received document bytes (#1263), but core v0.11.0 predates the per-type maxDocumentBytes check (#1251). Requiring v0.11.1 puts it in force. proof and capabilityclient move to v0.11.1 too.

New tests in both modules: a document over its type's bound from an authenticated sender is answered malformedRequest to that sender, the handler does not run, and the replay record stays empty, so the same id within the bound is then handled.

title: feat(transports): delivery receipts, unconfirmable deliveries, and waking a recipient through its own mediator (VTI-TRN-042, VTI-TRN-060 – VTI-TRN-074, VTI-APV-024)
body:
Normative side of OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#2553 (cross-mediator delivery evidence) and #2663 (waking a task-consent approver that has no ACL entry). The wire types are in trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#1297: `messaging/receipt/0.1`, `messaging/wake/set/0.1`, `messaging/wake/request/0.1`, `push/register/0.3`, the TSP binding 0.2 `deliveryId`, and the DIDComm binding `delivery_id` header.

## Delivery receipts (`05-transports.md`, new subsection)

- **VTI-TRN-060**: a sender requests a receipt per message with a binding delivery id. The id is not derived from content, is never reused for another recipient, and stays the same on a retry.
- **VTI-TRN-061**: the receiver SHOULD send a receipt, and MAY decline. It sends one only on request, only to the transport-authenticated sender, and only after it holds the message durably and has deduplicated it (VTI-TRN-043). A receipt is never varied by the operation's outcome.
- **VTI-TRN-062**: a receipt counts as class 1 only when `confirms` matches the delivery id and the receipt's sender is the addressed party. Anything else is ignored silently. A receipt is never answered and never asks for a receipt itself.
- **VTI-TRN-063**: during the transition, the earlier `https://affinidi.com/delivery/1.0/receipt` form is accepted alongside the Trust Task form.
- **VTI-TRN-064**: at send time, a sender establishes which evidence classes the path offers. Class 1 requires a recipient known to send receipts. Class 3 requires the sender's own mediator to hold the message. The sender polls for no class it has established is unavailable.

## VTI-TRN-042 amended

Where no evidence class was available on the path, the sender MAY record the delivery as **unconfirmable** and need not escalate. Escalation still applies to recipients known to send receipts. An unconfirmable delivery is reported neither as delivered nor as failed. The rationale is added.

## Waking a recipient (`05-transports.md`, new subsection)

- **VTI-TRN-070**: a node with no wake binding for a peer wakes it only through the peer's own mediator, with a request naming the messages it queued. It never holds the peer's handle.
- **VTI-TRN-071**: the request and the wake it causes are contentless.
- **VTI-TRN-072**: a pending request is not re-rung, including when the sender polls for status. The mediator rings at most once per message.
- **VTI-TRN-073**: holding a wake handle grants no authority to wake.
- **VTI-TRN-074**: the mediator gives the same answer whatever it did, and the requester sends without waiting on it. A mediator that refuses the type means no wake, not an error.
- **VTI-APV-024** (`03b-approvals.md`): applies these rules to named approvers. No standing is required to be woken, there is no re-wake while a request is pending, and waking confers no authority.

## Also

- Considerations: item 11 is extended and a new item 12 covers receipts as a presence signal. The later items are renumbered.
- Appendix F.3: three *observed* rows at VTI `17f913de7`, for VTI-TRN-060–063, VTI-TRN-064/042 and VTI-TRN-070–074/APV-024.

Rendered locally with `npm run render` (no errors).

title: refactor(vtc)!: one typed routing table for every Trust Task family; routes/ is the HTTP surface only
body:
Two structural refactors of `vtc-service`, in the order `docs/05-design-notes/vtc-service-decomposition.md` gives them: the rest of #2579 (one routing style), then #2574 (`routes/` stops being the operations layer). Rooms handlers are untouched (#2575 moves them). ## #2579 — one typed `AsyncDispatcher` for every family - `trust_tasks::routing`: one `AsyncDispatcher` every family registers on, keyed on the generated payload type (`on!(routes, P => handler)`). Each family exposes `register(Routes) -> Routes`. Every `URIS` constant, every family `dispatch`, the `FAMILIES` table and the ~60 direct arms of `dispatch_typed` are gone; `dispatch_typed` is now rooms → git-ns → the table → discovery. - The 540-line hand-kept `DISPATCHED_URIS` is replaced by `dispatched_uris()`, read off the table (version hints, discovery, size gate, censuses). It had already drifted: `auth/step-up/requests/show/0.1` was routed but not listed, so discovery never advertised it — **the one observable change in this part**. Before deleting the list, a temporary test held the registered set equal to it (that was the only difference). - Handlers are registered on `Received

`: routed and spec-policed as `P`, but handed the JSON as received, so (a) every handler still reads it against the schema before parsing it, and (b) administrative handlers still resolve the signer's authority **before** reading the payload — a typed downcast in the router would have reversed that and changed which refusal a stranger gets. - Families whose verbs share a pre-payload authority check (backup, website, administrator passkeys) route through a small `Op` enum rather than a URI match. - Censuses: no URI is registered twice; none is also a rooms/git-ns task. - `seed_acl`: the three copies (`trust_tasks::test_fixtures`, `git_ns::tests`, `acl::console_key` tests) now share `test_support::{seeded_acl_entry, seed_acl}`; the trust-task fixture keeps its legacy-context form over the shared entry, git-ns adds the member record it needs. ## #2574 — `routes/` is the HTTP surface only **Move** (pure, history kept): the 34 operations-only files left `routes/` for their domain modules — `acl::ops`, `auth::admin_passkeys`, `audit_ops`, `backup::ops`, `ceremony::listing`, `community::ops::{branding,config,did_register,join_discovery,profile,requested_attributes,theme}`, `endorsement_types::ops`, `endorsements::ops`, `install::ops::{…,bootstrap,invites}`, `join::{invitations,ops::*}`, `members::ops::*`, `policy::ops::{admin,read}`, `recognition::{recognise,admin}`, `registry::admin`, `relationships::ops`, `schemas::ops`, `vetting::{ops,hidden}`, `website::ops::*`. The public half of `community/profile` was split back into `routes/`. `routes/` now holds only what it mounts: the Trust Task door, the declared `REST_EXCEPTIONS`, WebAuthn, health, the public reads, the member portal and console assets (and `rooms.rs`, left for #2575). **Generated payloads**: the operations take the `vti_specs` payloads; the REST-era parallel structs and their `utoipa` derives are deleted — `ListMembersQuery`, `ListJoinRequestsQuery`, `IssueInvitationBody`, `endorsement_types::{ListQuery, RegisterBody}`, `AuditQuery`, `CreateInviteRequest`, `UpdateMemberRequest`, `RemoveBody`, `rotate::{ChallengeBody, FinishBody}`, `endorsements::IssueBody`, `RegisterSchemaBody`, `SendQueryRequest`, `policies::{ListPoliciesQuery, PolicyStatusFilter, ActiveQuery, UploadBody, TestBody}`, `RequestVmcBody`. Internal parameter structs that are built, never parsed (`PatchRequest`, `DecideBody`, `CheckQuery`, `BootstrapRequest`) lose their `Deserialize`/`utoipa` derives. Two places the generated type folds "absent" into "empty" (`members/update`'s `extensions`, `endorsement-types/register`'s `claimSchema`) read presence from the received JSON (`crate::wire::sent`) — the reason the double parse existed, now explicit. `crate::wire` reads generated enum members as domain types through their shared wire form. **Census**: `trust_tasks::payload_type_census` — every `let x: T = match parse_payload(&doc)` (and the `without_ext` form) in a handler must be a generated `…Payload`; a shrink-only baseline lists the rest with why. `vta-sdk/tests/generated_wire_types_census.rs`'s baseline paths follow the move. **Console**: `openapi.json` and `wire.ts` regenerated — `CreateInviteRequest`, `IssueInvitationBody`, `RequestVmcBody`, `PolicyStatusFilter` go (no console code used them); `RegisterBody` becomes `VtcEndorsementTypesRegisterV0_1Payload` (new `vta_sdk::openapi::EndorsementTypeRegister01Payload`), and `wire-types.ts` names it. `npm run typecheck`, `npm test` (1614) and `wire:check` pass. `vtc-service/CLAUDE.md`'s source layout is rewritten (it still called `routes/` "every HTTP route handler" and omitted a dozen modules), with a "where code goes" rule; operator docs' paths updated. ### Behaviour Unchanged except: discovery/version hints list `auth/step-up/requests/show/0.1` (always served); `policy/list` accepts an explicit `enabledOnly: false` (the schema default, asking for no filter — it used to be refused alongside `true`); a few `malformedRequest` messages for members the schema already constrains read differently (e.g. a non-UUID `rotationId`). Codes are unchanged. ### Claims checked - #2574 "the census does not scan vtc-service": **not so** — it scans every workspace member, and its baseline already listed vtc-service types. What it could not see is the validate-then-reparse pattern, which is what the new census covers. - #2579 "Not checked: whether a census pins `URIS` to `dispatch`": each family's `dispatch` ended in `_ => return None` and the router `unreachable!`ed on a mismatch, so a forgotten arm would have panicked at runtime; registration-by-type removes the pair entirely. ### Not done, deliberately - `ImportRequest` (`vtc/config/import`) and `CommunityProfileUpdate` stay: they are the export document's / storage layer's own model, not REST bodies. `relationships::ops::PublishBody` (a signed VRC, parsed as received) and `vetting::hidden::PublishHiddenVettingBody` (`vetting-pcs`; the generated type folds absent/empty lists and carries `tickLength`, which this body refuses) stay for their own PRs. The SDK's join/credential-exchange bodies stay (SDK census). All are in the new census's baseline with the reason. - `routes/auth.rs` keeps the session operations `admin_tasks` calls (`list_sessions_for`, `revoke_sessions_task`, …) beside the cookie routes they share code with; `routes/health.rs` keeps `diagnostics` beside `/health`. ### Breaking `vtc-service`'s public module paths moved (`routes::join_requests` → `join::ops`, `routes::recognise` → `recognition::recognise`, `routes::vetting_hidden` → `vetting::hidden`), hence `!`. `vta-sdk` gains one wrapper type (additive). Closes #2579 Closes #2574
